Mr. Robertson, Parliamentary Assistant, for the Minister of National Health and Welfare: Mr. Speaker, questions 64, 65 and 66 all deal with the same subject matter. With your consent, I will answer these three questions at this time.
Question No. 64 reads:
What is the total amount of federal funds allocated to: (a) construction costs; (b) equipment costs, for the Vancouver general hospital in the last 16 years, and how many more federal dollars are committed?
Since the establishment in 1948 of the national health program federal assistance for construction and for the provision of technical and scientific equipment in buildings and services on the grounds of the general hospital, Vancouver, has totalled as follows: (a) for construction costs, payments, $716,456; further commitments, $612,561; (b) for equipment costs, payments, $336,500; further commitments, $25,900.
Question 65 reads:
In connection with civil defence planning, will the Minister of National Health and Welfare consider the importance of decentralizing major hospital construction from Vancouver to those areas outside the boundaries of the city of Vancouver?
The problem of decentralizing hospital construction has received continuous study for many months, and is still under consideration. The damaging effect of high-yield nuclear weapons covers a radius which would make buildings uninhabitable for 15 miles from the explosion centre. Little protection would be afforded by sites on the fringe of cities, although the reduced damage at that distance might enable hospitals to be repaired and reoccupied as opposed to those within five to 10 miles of the centre of the city, which would likely be destroyed.
On the other hand, many staffing and other difficulties affect the practicability of completely rural location. Question No. 66 is as follows:
Is it not time to reassess the requests of the government of British Columbia to further enlarge the Vancouver general hospital, having in mind civil defence in British Columbia?
During the past year the province of British Columbia submitted a project under the national health program in respect of a proposed addition to the Vancouver general hospital. This project was approved by the federal government and assistance was made available in the amount of $609,236 for an addition of 524 beds and related facilities at that hospital. Since that time no further project relating to the Vancouver general hospital has been received from the province of British Columbia. Planning for the size, location and construction of public hospitals is of course the responsibility of the provincial governments concerned.

The house in committee on Bill No. 449, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act- Mr. Gregg-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 1

Extension of act to fishermen.

When this bill was considered yesterday by the standing committee on industrial relations, Mr. Chairman, there was a great deal of discussion, and I think useful discussion. When we had finished with the discussion members of the committee realized that the printed copy of the proceedings might possibly not be available until this house rises. Since I had made only a brief statement on the proposed change under section 45 (2) of the act at the (Mr. Fulton.]
resolution stage, the committee asked if I would make a slightly longer explanation when the bill came back into the house, and that, Mr. Chairman, I would ask leave to do.
First, this bill will enable the commission, with the approval of the governor in council, to bring under the act by regulation those engaged in the fishing industry. This part of the bill is to enable a decision now reached with respect to fishermen to be carried into effect during the coming months. The intention is to have the plan ready so that the contributions from fishermen for unemployment insurance might begin to be received on April 1, 1957, and the benefits therefrom available to those who qualify starting in April, 1958.
The second part of the bill is designed to ease the qualifying conditions for drawing benefits under section 45 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1955, and because of the inter-related nature of the act one or two other amendments are required as a consequence. I should like to explain the existing 1955 qualifying formula, the results which the formula has produced in the past year and the amendments we are now proposing to make in order to ameliorate those results.
Under section 45 (1) of the 1955 act a claimant, to establish his ordinary benefit period, must have at least 30 weeks' contributions in the 104 weeks preceding the date of his claim, and of those at least eight contributions must be in the 52 weeks preceding his claim or since his last benefit period began, whichever is the shorter period. Section 45 (2) of the 1955 act applies to subsequent claims for ordinary benefits, and I might mention a subsequent claim is one that is made within 104 weeks of the establishment of a previous claim.
Section 45 (2) requires the claimant to have made 30 weekly contributions in the 52 weeks immediately preceding the claim, or since the start of the last benefit period, whichever period is the greater. This section particularly affects groups of workers whose type of work results in their having to claim unemployment insurance benefit every 12 months. To these workers, section 45 (2) means that they have to find 30 contribution weeks every year and there are many who cannot do that. I shall deal more fully with this group in a few minutes.
In addition to these two aspects of ordinary benefit, the 1955 act provides for two classes of seasonal benefit. The concept of seasonal benefit was introduced into our unemployment scheme in recognition of the fact that we have had winter unemployment problems

of some magnitude. Consequently, it is payable only between January 1 and April 15, the period when it is difficult for an unemployed person to find work. It applies to those who are unable to qualify for ordinary benefit.
To qualify for class A seasonal benefit, a claimant must have 15 weekly contributions since the previous March. Class B seasonal benefit is payable to a claimant who has had an ordinary benefit period that has terminated since the previous April 15. Class B seasonal benefit is payable even though the claimant has not been able to contribute to the scheme since his ordinary benefit period expired. The theory here is that if he was unable to findi work during the spring, summer and autumn, he would be highly unlikely to find it during winter.
Now that I have talked about the qualifying formula that was evolved for the 1955 act, I would like to outline the results of actual practice that were observed in the months following October 2 last year when the new act came into effect. With section 45 (1) there was no difficulty. Indeed, a claimant filing his first claim can hardly have any real attachment to insured employment if he was not required to work at least 30 weeks in the last two years, with eight of them in the last year. By a worker with a "real attachment to insured employment" I mean a worker who is actually at work requiring insurance stamps.
In regard to section 45 (2), certain difficulties arose. This section provided that if a claim is made every year, the claimant, on his second and each following claim, can qualify only if he has 30 contributions in the 52 weeks preceding his new claim. This means that a worker whose job begins in the spring and who is laid off and claims benefit each year in November, for instance ,can qualify for ordinary benefit only if he has made at least 30 weekly contributions since the previous November. This applies in the same way, of course, to claimants whose layoff period comes at other times of the year. We feel now, from the experience gained, that this disposition works too great a stringency on a number of workers who, although their employment is less than year-round, nevertheless have a very substantial attachment to insurable employment. Because of these limitations that our climate imposes on certain industries, many persons who must of necessity confine their work to those industries are unable to get as many as 30 weeks of insurable employment in a year.
During the four months after the 1955 act went into operation, that is, the months of 67509-4574
Unemployment Insurance Act October, November, December, 1955, and January, 1956, the number of claimants who failed to qualify was 45 per cent of all those filing initial claims, as compared with 29 per cent in the same four months a year before. Most of this increase was caused by section 45 (2). The number of persons involved was, as I told the house last April 18, over 90,000. It is true, of course, that some 90 per cent of these workers had enough contributions to qualify for seasonal benefit beginning on January 1 of this year.
It is also a matter of record that the percentage of those failing to qualify levelled off in the winter to about the same ratio as in the previous winter. This shows that between October and January there is a considerable volume of claims from persons who have a spring-summer-autumn pattern of employment.
To sum it up, where the difficulties occurred was among those who work for periods just slightly shorter than 30 weeks each year, and in particular among groups who tend to suffer lay-offs at times of the year when they cannot draw seasonal benefits. It is these workers to whom our present amendment will apply.
I shall now explain the details of this amendment. I made a statement to the house last May 16 in which I suggested that the difficulties of claimants were aggravated by the interposition of a seasonal benefit period between two claims for ordinary benefit. I indicated then that we might take action along the lines of disregarding seasonal benefit periods for the purpose of section 45 (2). Further study has shown, however, that we can achieve the same result by a sounder method.
We are amending section 45 (2) so that, in addition to the general requirements of the present section 45 (1), only 24 of the required 30 contribution weeks need be in the past 52 weeks; or since the beginning of the last benefit period, whichever period is longer. By amending the requalifying requirements to this extent, a substantial number of those who failed to qualify for ordinary benefit last fall will find themselves able to qualify this fall.
The minimum period of benefit, as a result of lowering the number of qualifying weeks to 24, will of course be 12 weeks rather than 15 weeks, as before. Under this formula we find that of those claimants who, according to our survey last November, had only 24 to 29 weekly contributions, and thus failed to qualify for ordinary benefit, there will be 14-5 per cent who qualify for 15 weeks of benefit; 37-4 per cent who qualify for 14 weeks of benefit; 38-8 per cent who

Unemployment Insurance Act qualify for 13 weeks of benefit; and 15-3 per cent who qualify for 12 weeks of benefit; that is, almost 85 per cent of these workers would have benefit durations of 13 weeks or more.
This is a very closely inter-related act. In order to prevent certain anomalies arising because of this change we must also amend Section 53 (3)(b) and section 53(5). This is the section dealing with seasonal benefits. Section 53 (3)(b) is amended so that, for seasonal benefit class A, the duration would be one week for every two weekly contributions since the previous March, with a floor of 10 weeks. Unless this change is made, the present rule, which allows two weeks of benefit for every three weekly contributions, would result in an anomaly as between recipients of regular benefit and seasonal benefit.
Section 53 (5) is amended so that, for seasonal benefit class B, the duration would be based on that of the last ordinary benefit period. That is, the minimum would be 12 weeks and, since payment is limited to the period January 1 to April 15, the maximum would not exceed 16 weeks.
Since 1950 I cannot recall a single month in which the commission has not brought before me the results of serious study of this act, or of its regulations or of its administration. It is good legislation and deserves that constant review and improvement that can only be based on experience, and I promise that the review will continue.
As the minister responsible for reporting on the administration of the act to the house, I am grateful for the interest, criticisms and suggestions of members from all parts of the house which help to make it a valuable stabilizing influence within our economic life and, more important, a most important agency for serving the human needs of so many of our Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, we went over this bill in committee yesterday, as the minister said. I noticed that the minister said a few minutes ago the act was under constant review by the officials of his department. As all will agree who have had anything to do with the Unemployment Insurance Act, this is a complicated piece of legislation and its administration requires work of a very high and expert order. So the officials of the department are constantly reviewing the application of the act and the results of operations under the act.
In so far as section 29 is concerned, which is being amended by this bill to provide coverage for fishermen, there is unanimous opinion that this amendment should be made.
IMr. Gregg.]
We are glad to see it now although we feel that maybe it has been delayed a little. The matter has been under active consideration by this house since 1950 in any event and probably before that. I took the trouble last evening to go back over some of the discussions which have taken place. While practically every hon. member of the house who has any connection at all with fishermen has had something to say on the matter at one time or another, I should like to draw particular attention to one or two statements which have been made by members of my own group.
I recall that as early as 1950 when the hon. member for Royal was speaking in the unemployment insurance debate he drew attention to the plight in which both the fishermen and farmers in his district found themselves where they were engaged chiefly in seasonal employment at various times of the year. At that time he asked that some consideration be given to the plight of these men who were out of employment for extended periods of time. We hope that the regulations which will follow the passage of this bill and the work which the department will do in investigating conditions under which these men work in various parts of the country will result in adequate coverage for them.
It is true that conditions in the fishing industry on the east coast are different from those on the west coast. In so far as my own experience is concerned, peculiarly enough I have had more to do with the west coast. I have had more opportunity to study the conditions under which those men are employed. These men are protected by collective bargaining agreements to a much greater extent than those who operate on the east coast.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich from time to time has asked for protection for the workers in his locality. I recall that he has asked for protection, not only for the fishermen themselves but for those engaged in ancillary occupations. In 1954, speaking to the proposal that there should be a committee to inquire into the conditions of employment, he referred to the fact that government regulations had been introduced which affected the employment of men engaged in the logging and fishing industries. He referred to the need of greater research to make sure that our forests were not cut down in a comparatively short space of time. He then went on to refer to the fishermen and the fact that international regulations covering the fishing industry forced the men employed in that industry to work at selected seasons of the year. The hon. member then went on to say that it seemed to him that

when the committee was considering the matter consideration should be given to measures which could be introduced to offset seasonal unemployment.
He went on to ask that regulations should be brought in to ensure that those who were not in insured employment should have recourse to the benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Act. This matter came up last year when different hon. members spoke to it, and I refer particularly to the hon. member for Saint John-Albert and the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. I should like to refer to the remarks made last year in this house by the latter hon. member. The hon. member said, as many of us have said, that it must be admitted that there were grave difficulties in the way of including fishermen in the act but he pointed out that other countries had managed to get around those difficulties. He then went on to refer to the commission which had made a study of the industry and had reported back. He said that if that commission had found that the administrative difficulties could be overcome then the minister could submit to parliament machinery which could include this group of men within the framework of the act and overcome the difficulties which his officials had admitted could be overcome.
That was one of the striking things that came out of the consideration given to this matter by the committee last year, that while it was admitted the difficulties were grave it would be possible to overcome them. We are happy to welcome this bill which we hope will solve the problem for these men. There is one question the minister might like to answer when he replies. He has spoken of the studies which must be made by the department and has stated that commencing next year at the end of the present fiscal year they hope to be in position to start taking contributions and that benefits would then be available early in 1958. I wonder if the minister would tell us what effect the coming into force of the act on September 30 this year will have on the proposal to study the matter and commence contributions next year? Will there be any conflict between the effective date of the act and the time it is estimated will be required to make a study of the proposals with regard to fishermen?
I should like to say a few words with regard to the amendments proposed to section 45 and the other sections which require to be adjusted in conjunction therewith. Yesterday in the committee we studied some charts which some of us had seen previously which had been prepared by the department showing the effect of the amendments proposed. I must admit that the charts which were
Unemployment Insurance Act produced were very convincing. They gave a clear picture of what was expected this coming season with the amendments now being introduced. I would just like to say that, while those charts were convincing and while they set out the situation with regard to the three or four cases that were studied and were used as examples, it will, after all, be actual practice that will tell the tale. I do not suppose that even the officials of the department can predict what may happen this coming winter, because no two applicants ever have precisely the same pattern of employment; consequently, the same situation cannot be expected to obtain for even two persons, let alone the great number disqualified last year.
I was rather amused, reading in the newspapers the reports of the discussions that have taken place with regard to this act, to notice that in one newspaper at least the heading claimed that 100,000 persons would benefit under these revisions, whereas the very highest figures quoted in this house officially were that only some 90,000 had suffered by reason of the 1955 act, that a good many of these had been taken care of in one way or another by the revised interpretation.
Some 90 per cent.

Either the claims of some of the members of this house that the number was considerably in excess of 90,000 are now borne out or the number was a great deal exaggerated in so far as the present report is concerned. In any event, whatever the numbers may be, we hope that this revision or the amendment to 45 (2) will effect the desired result and that this coming winter we shall not have a recurrence of the situation with which we were faced last year.
1 cannot close these remarks without reiterating once more the request I have made to the minister twice already, that there be no delay at all in reviewing the effects of these amendments when they come into force and that the slightest inclination to slide again into the rut in which we found ourselves last winter will bring immediate action on the part of the minister and his officials.

I should like to reply, if I might, quite briefly to the special question the hon. member asked, namely, what significance the date of September 1 had upon the receiving of contributions and the paying of benefits. It has none whatsoever upon that. The reason why it was set as early as possible was that that would make it possible for us to evolve the regulations provided for under those two subheadings,

Unemployment Insurance Act that they may be completed before the final plan is crystallized. It was felt that the sooner that could be done the better. Consequently, September 1 was chosen as the date when this would come into effect.
Can we be assured that contributions will definitely be taken starting on April 1 of next year, whether or not the department has completely finalized its plans?

We are intending to complete the plans so that contributions may begin to be received on the first day of April 1957, the beginning of the next fiscal year and, as a result of that, that benefits may be payable to those that qualify after January 1, 1958.

As has been already stated, at various stages of the discussion on this bill, I think there is a thorough understanding that it is not a last-minute idea on the part of members of this house. 1 know that certain of the proposals in clause 1 of the bill to bring in coverage for the commercial fishermen will be welcomed not only by the commercial fishermen on the British Columbia coast but by those in the fresh water areas of Canada and in the Atlantic coast areas as well.
Perhaps it is one of the interesting situations in respect to our Unemployment Insurance Act that the change that this clause introduces has been brought about with a good deal less thunder on the floor of the house than has been considered necessary in respect to some other matters that we discuss here from time to time. In saying that, however, I think I should make it clear that I know-and certainly my colleague for Cape Breton South would verify-that this problem of fishermen has been of very serious concern to members such as the member for Cape Breton South ever since the first discussions on the Unemployment Insurance Act took place as far back as 1940.
However, I think it is a tribute to the attitude that has been taken by the unemployment insurance commission that, by making thorough studies of the problems, administrative and otherwise, that were involved, we are able to be discussing a clause such as the one before us today. It should be said that it has been in large part a co-operative effort between the commission, the minister and the members of the house who were particularly interested in this problem because of its existence in the areas of Canada from which they come.
I do not intend to prolong this discussion at any length, because we did give it a going over yesterday in the committee on industrial gelations; but we should appreciate that


clause 1 of this bill does make what to me is a rather significant change in the concept of the application of unemployment insurance as we have known it in this country up to the present time, inasmuch as for the first time it does bring in the principle of applying unemployment insurance to workers in this country who have not the employee-employer relationship in the narrow sense of that situation. I believe that that is a significant change that we should realize we are making at this time.
Much has been said about the administrative difficulties of bringing coverage to fishermen. I think the minister, as well as some of us not having administrative responsibilities, is aware of the fact that the passage of this bill is not going to eliminate all of those difficulties overnight. Some of us might be desirous of seeing this change become effective at an earlier date than next April. However, I think that those of us who understand some of the problems that the commission has been considering will be willing to suggest to fishermen who may be slightly disappointed that it is not going to come into effect tomorrow, that in the long run that may be to their benefit. I certainly hope that that will prove to be the case.
I have made special reference to this new concept which is coming into the act, because I think that out of the administrative experience that will result from the application of this provision to fishermen it will be possible in the not far distant future to extend the application of that idea to some of the other areas of activity in our country that so far have been outside the scope of unemployment insurance. I have in mind particularly, of course, the quite large group of agricultural workers in this country who are still not covered by unemployment insurance. As the minister will recall, that problem was discussed to a considerable extent in the committee last year when we were undertaking a complete review of the act. Certain changes were made with regard to the coverage regulations which nibbled at the fringes of the problem of the agricultural workers. However, it has been drawn to my attention recently that because of the gradual extension that has taken place in the coverage of working people by unemployment insurance and the fact that we have a relatively high level of employment throughout the country at the present time, quite a number of farmers are having some difficulty in securing all the agricultural help they would like, and one of the reasons given for that is that people do not want to go to work in uninsured employment.
I throw that out at this time because I feel it is a problem we should not forget and

also to indicate, of course, that in my view the Unemployment Insurance Act is not perfect yet. I hope that the minister and the commission will continue to give serious consideration to the possibility of extending coverage to workers in the agricultural field and that they will have that in the back of their minds as they gain administrative experience in the administration of the coverage of fishermen.
While I am on my feet, perhaps I might make some reference to the change being made in section 45(2). I am not going to attempt to discuss it in detail. Here again I think I can say that I am glad to see that the change being brought about in section 45(2) at this session is an indication that the commission and the minister are prepared to take a somewhat flexible attitude with respect to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I hope that attitude will continue because I think it has been made abundantly clear that it is not too easy to foresee in advance the implications of all the changes that are made in the act, and the introduction of section 45(2) into the act last year certainly had results which I think no member of the industrial relations committee last year fully foresaw and which I think the minister and the commission by their own admission have indicated that they did not expect.
Therefore, while I believe that after the discussion we had yesterday all members of the committee are convinced that the proposal being brought forward here is going to correct in large measure a weakness revealed last winter in respect of section 45(2), nevertheless we will still continue to attempt to analyse the effect of the changes that are now being made. We hope that if it should prove to be the case that some inequities still result from the changes now being made the minister will be prepared to take the initiative in introducing future changes in the legislation. I know that the thought in the back of the minds of some members of the industrial relations committee last year when we were making a complete overhaul of the Unemployment Insurance Act was, that that was going to be "it", probably for some time. I recall that the minister did give us some reason last year to believe that it might be sometime before he would be willing to open up the act again.
I was an optimist.

I am glad to see that was not a hard and fast approach as far as he was concerned. The present bill does make some changes in respect of the application of the seasonal benefit plan, and if it should happen that experience proves that those changes are working out to the serious disadvantage
Unemployment Insurance Act of any appreciable number of workers I hope the minister will be willing to take a second look at the situation when we come back again.
I think I have made it clear that more and more the Unemployment Insurance Act and the unemployment insurance fund are coming to be regarded as one of the greatest social assets we have in this country, something to be protected and guarded zealously by the working people of Canada and something which can be approached from the point of view of a careful analysis of the economics that are involved in it. As far as we are concerned, and I know I speak for all my colleagues when I say this, we intend to continue to press for changes in the act as we think they are required from time to time in order to make it more nearly the ideal coverage against the hazard of unemployment that it should be.

Mr. Chairman, in speaking again on Bill No. 449, now that it is back in the house in the committee stage, may I say that we in this group are pleased indeed that the committee saw fit to accept it in its present form. The enabling legislation found in clause 1 is particularly gratifying, as I indicated in my earlier address. However, when examined it raised a question in my mind with respect to its relationship to the other amendment having to do with section 45(2) and the actuarial soundness of the plan in the future.
We must remember that this year has been the peak period of employment in this country. I am satisfied that the fishermen desire immediate inclusion under the terms of the act. Those of us who were members of the industrial relations committee realize that this is not a simple problem and that it is going to take some study before they can be included if the fund is not going to be affected to the detriment of those in the country as a whole who may desire unemployment insurance. However, I should not like to see the government use the excuse that it is hard to work out the details as a reason for procrastination in putting into effect the terms of the legislation and including fishermen at an early date.
In discussing the bill, and having regard to the actuarial soundness of the fund, we found that last year, which was, as I said earlier, the peak period of employment in the country, the actual unemployment insurance fund as such would have been some $13 million in the red except for some very sound investments made under the fund itself which resulted in a revenue of $25 million and the fund therefore showing a profit of $12 million. If we were to have a depressed period

Unemployment Insurance Act in our economy such as we had in 1954 and having in mind the fact that fishermen are now to be included and that the broadening of section 45(2), it is estimated, may cost as much as $9 million, then on the basis of last year's figures the fact that this is a much improved piece of legislation over what we had even in the old act before 1955 will mean an additional demand on the fund of $9 million. In other words, while the fund this year showed a surplus of some $9 million because of the peak period of employment in the country, the addition of another $9 million charges that the fishermen put on it and $9 million through the implementation of the proposed revision of section 45(2) makes me rather dubious as to the soundness of the fund at the present time. That matter gives me the greatest concern at this time. I do not wish to take up any more time of the committee at this stage. I wanted to draw that matter to their attention because my feeling is-and I think industrialists and employees alike must realize it-that it may mean a revision upwards of the contributions, and it may also mean a later revision of the act, as I say, so as not to include such a large scope under its benefits.
As was indicated by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, we need unemployment insurance in this country in order to keep our economy buoyant. In order to have that unemployment insurance, we must keep our fund solvent at all times. I would urge the government to be extremely careful in implementing this new piece of legislation.

Mr. Chairman, on clause 1 I should like to refer to this important amendment which now includes the fishing industry. As the hon. member for Hamilton West has said, this step has been advocated for years in this house. We have always realized, of course, that there were in the way grave administrative problems which would have to be solved. Undoubtedly at least some of those solutions still lie ahead of us. I happened to turn back the pages in Hansard this morning and glance at the debates in 1952 when the then hon. member for St. John's East raised this matter and was discussing it with the minister. At that time the minister, as reported at page 1164 of Hansard of 1952, said this:
The nature of the industry, which is highly seasonal, makes it very difficult under present procedures and conditions to apply unemployment insurance even to the wage earners.
He had pointed out at that time that only 7 per cent of the total labour force, according to the latest statistics at that time, were actually wage earners. Others were masters and owners, sharesmen and lone workers. Then the minister went on to say this:


As my hon. friend knows, the difficulties which I have outlined apply with special emphasis to the Atlantic coast fishing industry.
There is no doubt that on the east coast there is a problem which is going to require a great deal of patience and a great deal of forethought to overcome and in order to have this matter work out equitably and well. Nevertheless, as I pointed out a year ago when speaking on this matter, the United States, although at first dubious about it, finally brought in unemployment insurance for fishermen and it has apparently worked reasonably well. In Britain, where they refused to do it for many years, it was brought in almost ten years ago and it has worked there, as well as in some European nations such as, I believe, Holland and Norway. Hence, given good will and co-operation on both sides-and when I say "both sides" I mean the administration on the one end and the industry on the other-there should not be too much trouble in solving this problem.
I think the situation which arises is perhaps necessary but rather unfortunate; but since this matter is now to the fore we must face it. The minister told us this morning that the contributions will start next April, I think it is, and that the benefits will be payable at the beginning of January, 1958. It is quite a long while to wait. In other words, seven or eight years will have expired from the time this matter was first raised in the house. I recall that Gordon Higgins, the then hon. member for St. John's East, raised this matter and discussed it even before the reference to it which I made a little while ago. Hence it has been a subject of discussion for at least six years now. Another two years will elapse before it finally comes into effect. But it is something which, I understand, will be of incalculable benefit to the fishing industry. It is something which is badly needed.
I want to commend the minister and the officials of his department who have given this matter a great deal of study and have listened to the representations which have been made in this house. We are at least embarking now on a road which, although there are going to be a good many hills, some ditches and probably a few boulders to surmount, will in the end, I think, straighten out and provide a method of assistance to the industry which will contribute to the economy of Canada as a whole.

Mr. Chairman, I should just like to interject a word or two at this point in the discussion. I think it would be only fair to say that members supporting this government, either in the house or outside

the house or both, have also pressed that a plan such as this be made possible.

Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to prolong the discussion on this matter. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni said practically everything that I would say and there is no need of repeating it. However, I should like to say this with respect to the question of fishermen being brought under the act. When the act was set up in 1940 I was a member of the house. A committee of this house worked that act over for some considerable time. At that time a proposal was made as to the advisability of bringing fishermen under the act. Having had no experience with unemployment insurance in the country most of the members of the house at that time, including that committee, were reluctant to try to include fishermen until such time as the commission had been set up, had functioned and, as a result of that experience, it could be determined whether it was practical or otherwise to bring the fishermen in.
Up until the last few years most of us were doubtful whether fishermen could be included. Of course there would be no difficulty where the trawlers are operating and are marketing their fish at fish plants. That is something that is relatively simple. But there is a large group of fishermen who are selfemployed; and it is going to take a little bit of manoeuvring and study to set up the mechanics that are necessary in order to include them. But with the experience the commission has now had and with the field workers they have plus the officials of the Department of Fisheries-the minister has many inspectors and others in the field who can greatly assist-I am reasonably sure that the unemployment insurance commission can set up the necessary machinery. I also think the amendment to section 45 (2) is going to bring considerable relief with respect to the problem we had last winter, but I am not going to go into that matter now. I merely wanted to identify myself with my colleague, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, and indicate support for the remarks that he made. I think he dealt with the matter very well and that there is no need of my taking up any more time of the committee.

Mr. Chairman, my views on this legislation are well known. I see no reason why I should take up the time of the committee at this time in repeating what I have already said previously on numerous occasions. On behalf of my constituents and of the fishermen of my province generally I merely wish to take this opportunity to express to the Minister of Labour and to his colleagues my appreciation for bringing in this legislation at this time.
Unemployment Insurance Act

Mr. Chariman, like other members of the house, I am glad to see this legislation come forward because it has been obvious for a long time that the fishermen should be included in the unemployment insurance program. Fishermen are faced with the same problems as those which are faced by other members of the working force when, through no fault of their own, they are unable to work and to provide for their families. As the hon. member for Hamilton West said this morning, the members of our party, along with other members of the house, have pressed for a number of years that this legislation should be brought forward, and we are glad to see that it has finally appeared. Fishermen play a very important part in, and make a great contribution to, our national economy and they should be allowed to contribute to and benefit from our unemployment insurance program like the other members of the working force. I regret that it will not be until January 1, 1958 that they can begin receiving benefits. However, I am glad to see the legislation coming forward, and I believe it is a good measure.

I wonder if I might interject a word here to the effect that this change in the contribution weeks from 30 to 24, while it is a step in the right direction, will not completely solve the problem of the dock workers at Saint John and to a slightly less degree in Halifax. We have received many representations and we know the seasonal difficulties which they face. We know, Mr. Chairman, that it is almost impossible for them, in view of the length of the season on the St. Lawrence now, to get in much more than 20 weeks. I say that this will help some of them, and it is a step that will relieve the situation for part of the group that found themselves in difficulty under the act when it was changed. I simply put that reservation forward and say that we will have to watch their problem. They do not qualify under the seasonal benefits because of the length of their season during the year. They are under the divisor system at present, by their own choosing, but it also has shown more disparity under the new act than formerly.
We must continue to examine the qualifying period and also the rates of benefit for this important group of workers in our maritime economy. We appreciate the new legislation that will eventually bring in the fishermen to insurance benefits. They are going through a transitional period now, and as part-time workers are trying to build up their interest in this industry. It will be of assistance, as has been mentioned. I do not go along with the worries that have been

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration expressed by the hon. member for New Westminster. I feel that the problem he has suggested is one that is more for the actuaries.
I would suggest now that a fishing trip be provided to Newfoundland for the minister by the hon. member who has just spoken.

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 2 to 5 inclusive agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.
DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION Immigration branch-
65. Administration of the Immigration Act, $950,650.

Last evening at the adjournment I was just beginning to make a few observations with respect to the immigration laws as they affect Canadian citizens of East Indian origin. I had also indicated that I was speaking not only on my own behalf but on behalf of the other members of this group from British Columbia. We discussed these various matters, and we are in agreement.
I feel that Canadian citizens of East Indian origin should receive consideration by the minister and his department. We have a number of them, of course, in British Columbia. The great majority of them live in the lower mainland area and over on Vancouver island. These people are British citizens because they come from nations that belong to the British commonwealth of nations. They feel, and I believe they are justified in feeling this way, that they have been discriminated against so far as immigration requirements are concerned. I have had the privilege of getting to know a number of these people. I believe I can safely say that they are very industrious and law-abiding. In addition to that, considerable numbers of them become employers, and I feel that should be taken into consideration by the minister. They set up business, such as sawmills and other industries, and employ

a considerable number of workmen. I believe that in this way they make a very valuable contribution to the various communities in which they are located.
As we read the immigration Act and consider the regulations approved by order in council P.C. 1956/785 of May 24, 1956, we find that this discrimination is pointed out in a very graphic manner. Immigrants who have come from the various South American countries and also from Israel, Egypt, Lebanon and Turkey as well as some other peoples, are granted privileges that far exceed the privileges granted the citizens of East Indian origin. In addition, we find that the privileges that are granted to these people when they become residents of the country are not afforded the people of East Indian origin until they have become citizens of the country which follows after the five-year residence qualification is fulfilled. I believe that this is another regulation which should be considered, and some amendment introduced to take care of that discrimination.
I do not propose, Mr. Chairman, to deal at any further length with this particular subject, except to place on record a telegram which I just received this morning. It is signed by Kuldeep Singh Bains, the secretary of the East Indian-Canadian welfare association. This gentleman and two others came here just a short time ago as a delegation to present the views of the East Indian people. The telegram is as follows:
Further to our representation on July 12, 1956 re immigration regulations as they affect Canadian citizens of east Indian origin.
We respectfully request you to urge the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, the hon. J. W. Pickersgill, to allow entry into Canada of the close relatives of Canadian citizens of East Indian origin on the same basis and the same classes of people as from Europe, Middle East and Latin-America. We shall appreciate you taking up this matter during the present debate in commons on immigration estimates.
I do not think anything further needs to be said on this matter. The minister is aware of the problems and he is aware of the representations that have been made. This morning, I just want to place myself on record in this connection. I believe he is also aware of the support that we in this group are giving to their requests.

Mr. Chairman, I assure you I am not going to delay unduly the committee, but I want to put on record a few thoughts on what seems to be a very important subject, namely, that which has been referred to already by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat and by the hon. member for Vancouver East.
First, may I say that I take direct issue with the hon. member for Kamloops in his

reference to the minister's handling of individual cases. I do not know whether many members handle more immigration cases than I do myself. I 'certainly hope not, because if they all have as many as I have the minister must have a great many headaches indeed. I just want to say this for what it is worth. In all the cases that I have taken up with him he has shown an infinite capacity for taking pains; he never lets the letter of the law stand in the way of the humanitarian interest, and I find him guided indeed by that in which the hon. member for Kamloops said he was lacking, namely, the milk of human kindness. I have a letter on my desk this morning about the reunion of one particular family whose names I will not mention, but that one letter alone would repay, I think, in great measure the pains the minister took to get this particular case settled satisfactorily.
Second, I want to say that, in view of the fact that I do have a good many immigration cases, and indeed I had them before I was a member of this house, I think the minister deserves credit for the great improvement in the new regulations which were published on May 24 of this year. They are very much clearer and simpler and they go right to the heart and -cut through many of the worst difficulties which we had.
As I see it, as far as we in British Columbia are concerned, the most general grievance we get is that immigration from Asian Countries is not treated on the same basis as immigration from other countries. I think it is a very big and very complicated subject. I know also, in regard to Chinese immigration, we have that genial gentleman, Mr. Foon Sien, coming down here from Vancouver every year and putting up a very good case for the Chinese community of Canada. We know that matter is being very well handled and also, Mr. Chairman, if we examine the number of immigrants who come in we see that there is no real cause for complaint. On the general level the numbers who are actually coming in are very much higher than they were for many years.
I want to say just a few words in regard to the East Indian, and on this I am speaking, I think, for all of my Liberal colleagues from British Columbia. We have thought of this a great deal over many years; we have followed the different delegations that have been down. The one that was here this year, which I had the honour to accompany when it visited the minister, I thought was of the highest calibre of any delegation from British Columbia that has yet come from that particular community. So that we may clearly understand the problem, may I say the East Indian
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration community is comprised of about 2,000 men, women and children, most of whom have been in this country for a great many years. Incidentally, it is worth noting that over the years, whereas all the other communities we can think of, the Chinese community, the Ukrainian community, the German community, or any of the others that we can think of in terms of racial groups, have by and large increased, this is not true of the East Indian community because, by and large, they have just barely been able to hold their own. The number that has gone out has more than balanced the number that has come in and the natural increase.
I will not go into old unhappy history, and there were same very unhappy moments, as many of us will recall, particularly in 1914 when there was a very sensational, a very explosive episode, when someone tried to get in a whole shipload of East Indian immigrants at one particular time. Some members in this house will recall the agitation which almost led to steps to prevent that, but that is old, unhappy history, which could be and should be forgotten. I think it is fair to say-and I think the members of parliament of all four political parties representing British Columbia constituencies will bear me out when I say this-there is no community, there is no racial group of any kind, that has a better record for obedience to the law and for general unostentatious good citizenship than the East Indian group. You hardly ever hear of an East Indian being on relief. I admit you sometimes do hear of their being up in police court for driving their trucks too fast. That seems to be their most ostentatious bad habit. They are a family people. The vast majority of them are engaged in the woodworking business. Since they are a family people they place the newcomers according to a family basis.
I am sorry that the hon. member for Vancouver East is not in the house at the moment because, while I agree substantially with what he said about the treaty being too restrictive, I think perhaps he overlooks the fact-and I helped to get the treaty, by the way, because I had worked with the East Indians for many years, long before I became a member of parliament-that the treaty itself is a great forward step, and was hailed as a great forward step by the whole East Indian community of British Columbia as well as, of course, the government of India, because it gave the Indians what they had never had before, namely, at least some guaranteed right for a certain limited number of entries into Canada. But, in my opinion -and I am quite convinced that it is the opinion of a substantial majority of the
7202	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration members of parliament of all parties from British Columbia-the treaty as it now stands is too restrictive. The quota number from India is only 150 a year. That is too restrictive. If we take actual figures, Mr. Chairman, we will see that over the years they have not even got in the quota. Here again the minister deserves a great tribute for his personal attention to this particular problem. We did manage to clean up the great backlog of complicated cases of people who have been held up for a good many years that the minister did allow in more or less to wipe the slate clean. But we do find every year, when it comes to examining those who are going to come in under the 150 quota, there are just not enough places to go around and so it always ends in very keen and bitter disappointment to some of the East Indian community in British Columbia.
What I want to submit, Mr. Chairman, is this. I am not going to repeat anything about the brief; the minister knows all about it, and all the members from British Columbia know all about it because we have all read it, and I think all the members, without exception, gave letters of support to the East Indians from British Columbia. Certainly, if they did not give them direct support they did give moral support. I urge the minister to give earnest consideration to the relaxation of the general regulations in regard to immigration from India of those people of Sikh origin. Of course, everybody knows, or most people from British Columbia know, that all of our immigration from India is of Sikh religion. They all come from that one part of India; they all believe in one god. They are not idol worshippers. As a matter of fact, if we were to go far enough back we would find that they are of the same racial stock as we ourselves, if anyone is interested in that, although personally I am not.
I do believe that the general effect of the regulation is to make it too restrictive on immigration from India. I believe public opinion, in British Columbia particularly, would support a considerable relaxation in the quota provisions, if we have such a thing or whether or not we have a treaty. Personally I do not think a treaty is necessary. I think the treaty has outlived its usefulness. But whether or not we continue the treaty I do think we could easily absorb at least double the number of immigrants from East India that we have been absorbing, and perhaps even three times as many. I am sure we could do that without creating any problem of racial antagonism or unemployment or relief.
[Mr. Philpott.l

Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the Conservative members from British Columbia I should like to also urge upon the minister that he reconsider the provisions with regard to immigration from India. One significant fact is that India is a sister nation in the commonwealth and I think that should be borne in mind at all times.
Probably many hon. members of the house had the interesting privilege of interviewing the members of the delegation which was here last month representing the East Indian Canadian citizens welfare association. The three delegates were Tara Singh Bains, Narantan Singh Grewall and Rajindi Singh Mayo. All of these men are leaders in their communities. I had not been acquainted before with Tara Singh Bains but I had known or known of the other two.
Mr. Grewall came to Canada in 1926 and has established a substantial lumber business in the Fraser Valley. He has served on the municipal council of the area in which he resides and I believe is to be a candidate in the next provincial election. He has been an outstanding citizen. Just last year he built a school in his home village in India and he and his wife went there to attend the official opening which was done by Mr. Williams of the Canadian high commissioner's office in New Delhi. This year Mrs. Grewall is building a health centre adjacent to the school. This promotion of good feeling between Canada and India merits the highest praise.
Mr. Rajindi Singh Mayo is also an extremely interesting man. His father came here as an immigrant many years ago and established a large lumbering industry on Vancouver island. The father died within the last year or two and this young man who is in his early twenties is now the head of this business. If you please, he pilots his own private plane when he comes east, which he does on frequent occasions. I understand that his fellow representatives did not fly east with him, but he flew his own plane to come here to interview members of parliament.
These facts will give hon. members some idea of the type of citizens who are asking for reconsideration of the present provisions. They are particularly upset by the fact that people from Egypt, of which we have heard in the last few weeks, Lebanon, Turkey and the countries of Central and South America are in a preferred position. They appear to have more right to bring in their relatives than these people from a sister nation of the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
commonwealth. I do not think that is a proper situation. In the last paragraph of their brief they say:
Alternatively, we submit that as Canadian citizens the very least that we should ask for is that we should be treated no worse than Latin Americans and Levantines, and that we should be given the same rights that they are given as to bringing in relatives. We ask that regulation 21 be widened to let in relatives of Canadian citizens of East Indian origin, to the same extent as regulation 20 (c) admits Latin American and Levantine relatives.
I submit that that request is a reasonable one and I hope the minister can assure the committee today that there will be some change made in favour of these people who have proved themselves to be such worthy citizens of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I feel I must say a few words on this because it so happens that there are more East Indians in my constituency than in any constituency in Canada. I may say also that at one time I worked for the father of the young man to whom the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has referred. I might say that it was almost impossible to quit his employment because when any of his employees did quit he would come up from Victoria to find what in the world was wrong that had caused one of his men to leave his employ. There cannot be any doubt about the justice of their claim for freer admission to Canada. I think that has been proved quite fully.
There is another angle to this matter which I think we should consider. In our immigration policy we are of necessity dealing very closely with our relationships with other parts of the world. I submit that at this time it is essential that the relationships between the people of North America and of Asia should be strengthened in every possible way. I can think of nothing that would tend more to consolidate friendly feelings between our own part of the world and the new states of Asia than a more generous immigration policy for people from the new countries which have arisen in Asia during the last few years.
I think we should also consider this matter along these lines. While all of us of this generation pride ourselves on being free of racial prejudice, nevertheless all of us are more or less conscious of the great differences between the different families of the human race. But I think that state of mind is vanishing under the impact of modern ideas. In my own lifetime I have observed a tremendous change in the attitude of people toward those of other races. It may well be that within a few years the apprehension which is now quite widespread among the people of our particular branch of the human family about an influx of people from other branches of
the human family will appear to our grandchildren to have been rather fantastic and medieval. I do not think we should be a bit frightened about having people of other racial origins joining our national community.
For one thing I do not think there is going to be any tremendous influx. But I do think it would be of great importance to strengthen all commonwealth ties, and I think it would reduce the frictions felt by a section of the human family which has been exploited for many centuries if we were to adopt steps such as have been urged today.
Before I sit down I want to say another word with regard to immigration policy that I think is quite important. It seems to me that the minister has two jobs: one to encourage people to come to Canada and the other to keep certain people out. I have been wondering of late whether we are not spending too much time, too much energy and too much money on the latter function, to the detriment perhaps of the former function.
I have spoken to the minister about this matter on more than one occasion and suggested to him that, for instance, the elaborate steps that are taken to make sure that no subversive elements from eastern Europe reach our shores are ridiculous on two scores. The first score is that under the present regulations, people coming from eastern Europe and communist-dominated countries must manage somehow or other to get into western Europe and live there for two years before they can apply to come to Canada. As I have suggested to the minister on more than one occasion, a determined subversive element from a communist country who had been assigned the task of subverting our democratic way of life in Canada would think nothing whatever of that two years probationary period in western Europe in order to qualify to enter Canada.
I wonder whether the hon. gentleman does not think that these remarks would be more appropriate on the estimates of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice.

No, I do not think so, because these are matters of the regulations of the minister's department. Admittedly the minister calls on the Department of Justice, I believe, to aid him in this particular function, but it is primarily his function.
Then, as I have also suggested to the minister, I think it is quite naive of us to suggest that if a communist organization is going to send a spy or a subversive character who is going to upset our whole society he will come in here as an obvious resident of eastern Europe speaking with a strong foreign accent. In fact, as I suggested to the minister
7204	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration once, he is far more likely to come here with the very best social credentials and perhaps be a guest out at Rideau Hall. This is the kind of people that might be our most dangerous enemies. I think there is almost too much stress laid on the idea of attempting to screen people in regard to their ability to subvert our way of life, and I should like to see the minister be a little less careful in that regard and a little more careful in regard to the use of our immigration policy to enhance the friendly relations that we have with other parts of the world.

On the subject of immigration to Canada of relatives of East Indians who are Canadian citizens, I think that all the general principles applicable have been discussed and I shall not repeat them beyond indicating my support for what has been said. But I should like to ask the minister to deal, when he replies, with one problem which concerns us now and possibly will still be a problem even if the quota is relaxed or a more generous policy of admission is adopted. Under the present arrangment, of the number allowed to come in here from India, so many are assigned to the applications originating within India and so many to applications by Canadian citizens in Canada for the admission of their relatives from India. I have had two or three of them outstanding for, I am sure, three or four years. In discussions with the minister's officials, when I have been doing everything I can to put as much pressure as I can, I admit, to get these applications favourably considered, I have always had courteous treatment from the officials but unfortunately entirely negative results in the ones I now have in mind.
That has not always been true.

I say "in the ones I now have in mind." I have not had a uniformly negative result, but there are two or three that have stuck over the last few years. Although these are admissible on all other grounds there is just no room on the quota. If I understand the information correctly, and, as pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver South, there is room on the other branch of the quota, that is to say, the number assigned to applications originating in India, this, of course, creates great misunderstanding.
That has not been true in the past two years. The whole quota has been taken up in the past two years. It was true earlier.

I must have misunderstood the information. I thought it was still the situation. If the quota is to be enlarged or if the restrictions are to be relaxed, could the minister say what will be done to avoid that situation and also to avoid, where possible, the other bitterness that arises where these East Indians in Canada will come to their member and say, "I had my application for the admission of my nephew on file long before an application for another relative who I know has been admitted, and I have not yet had mine in"? I appreciate that it is difficult to work out a consecutive numerical priority because there are other factors that must be considered. All I shall say, therefore, is that the present situation gives rise to a great deal of dissatisfaction because a man is bound to be upset when, in discussing with a friend the admission of their relatives, he finds out that the other has had somebody admitted and the application was not submitted for some particular time after that for his own relative. I would appreciate it if the minister would say a word on those two aspects of the matter.

It is one minute before one o'clock, and I can say all I have to say in that time. I will try to get back to the subject but there are so many bypaths that it is so interesting to tread. To get back to the subject, I am not impressed, though I understand why the East Indian delegation is impressed, by their objections to East Indians being in category Cd) rather than in category (c) of the regulations of May 24. The reason I am not impressed is that these regulations confer no rights of any kind upon anybody. All they do is to indicate the categories of persons whose applications are considered by the department.
The fact that one of these people applies means nothing except that the application will be processed and if that person can satisfy all the requirements of the Immigration Act he will be admitted. I admit it does look on the face of it-and I am going to deal first with Egypt, Israel, Lebanon and Turkey-as though there were discrimination in favour of people from those countries compared with people from India until you stop to think that all these are are just criteria for admission. There are virtually no Egyptians in this country and the applications we do receive from Egypt are almost entirely from people who are not Egyptians but people who happen to be living there and who are English or French or in many cases Armenian in origin. In some cases, of course, they are Jews, people whose life in Egypt is more difficult than it has

The same thing applies to Turkey. There are practically no Turks in this country and there is no desire on the part of Turks to come here. But there are Armenians and other communities in Turkey where the people have relatives in this country, and it is just for administrative convenience that these two countries are in this category.
That is not quite true of Israel or Lebanon. However, there are special circumstances, quite often circumstances of a humanitarian character, and it is more convenient again not to have to ask for orders in council. That is the only reason. In the case of Lebanon, it is true we have quite a considerable number of Lebanese in this country. There are no large colonies but they are scattered over the country. According to my recollection, it is much smaller than the number of Indians who come, taking one year with another. I have not checked the figures this morning.
So far as the South American and Central American countries are concerned, the same thing is even truer. These countries are also countries of immigration and the local inhabitants very rarely come here as immigrants. But there are a certain number of refugees who have gone to South America at one time or another, particularly since the war, and who have relatives here. We could not take them right after the war because of shipping and other difficulties. Some of these people want to come here. We could easily strike all these countries out and deal with applicants by order in council, but it is a little more cumbersome. However, in any case no rights are conferred. It is just a matter of administrative convenience.

was no intention to discriminate in these matters in the sense of saying that some people are better than others. It is just an administrative device. I hate to hold up my own estimates, but I think I had better finish what I was saying when hon. gentlemen got so hungry at 1.15 they felt I should not continue.
I want now to say a word about Chinese immigration. As hon. members are well aware, there was practically no Chinese immigration from the time of the passing of the Chinese Immigration Act in 1923 until its repeal on May 14, 1947. Since that time the regulations respecting immigration from China have been the same as those respecting other countries in Asia. This was true until May 24 of this year when we took out of the regulations all references to persons of Asian racial origin, and geographical areas and actual countries were substituted in the regulations. This removed one anomaly which I must say troubled me a great deal. It was not a very important thing, but it was a source of annoyance to a certain num-oer of people. For instance, persons of east Indian and Chinese origin who were living, say in Trinidad, found it more difficult to get into Canada than persons of other origins in Trinidad and that did seem rather absurd, especially if the family had been there for several generations. That is no longer true.
From 1946 to 1955, including both years, there have been 14,104 Chinese immigrants landed in Canada which I think most hon. members will agree is a considerable number in 10 years. Now, from May 14, 1947 to December 18, 1950 the upper age limits of
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration these Chinese immigrants who were children of Canadian citizens was 18, and on December 28, 1950 it was raised to 21. Then, on June 28, 1951, my predecessor, the Minister of Finance, made a special concession whereby, in compassionate circumstances, he recommended to the governor in council that the governor in council should admit unmarried children of over 21 and under 25. This concession, though it was never part of the regulations and never part of the law, was continued until I announced in the estimates committee last year on March 10 that I did not propose to make any more such recommendations. I gave the reasons at that time, and I do not think there is any need to repeat them now. This was meant to cover a special situation and that special situation has I think really disappeared. Indeed, there has been very little protest about this change.
On the same day, I did indicate that special consideration would be given to applications for parents where the father was over 65 or the mother over 60. This has been formally incorporated into the regulations as of May 24, 1956. I may say that, though the numbers who have come have not been very large, this change was greatly appreciated, according to the information that has come to me, by the Chinese Canadian community. I think it is something that would commend itself to all hon. members, and I am glad to say that it is now part of the law.
Yesterday the hon. member for Vancouver East spoke about some of the difficulties he had had in some of his cases. I want to say at the outset that I very much appreciate the kind references with which he began his indictment of my administration. I may say there is no member on either side of the house with whom I find it pleasanter to deal than the hon. member for Vancouver East. I think you may describe us as a mutual admiration society most of the time, but we do have our differences. I want to speak about those points he raised. I must say I was just a little bit hurt-I would not have been if it had been anyone else-when the hon. gentleman said there was too much red tape in my department. I do not think anybody has done more to cut red tape than I, at any rate, have tried to do since I have been minister, particularly when I have been approached as seductively as I always am by the hon. gentleman.
The hon. gentleman did mention some sad cases where he had not been able to melt my heart or the hearts of the officials, and he raised some question as to whether I was a father. I did my best to give a demonstration of that in the gallery this morning and

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration I was very disappointed the hon. gentleman was not here to see it. My views on that subject are pretty well known. I want to explain quite seriously to hon. members why we did establish this rule to which the hon. gentleman took exception, that both parents must come into the country if the children are to be admitted. I do not say it was true of the great majority of Chinese Canadians, but it was true of a minority, that they found it more convenient to keep their wives in China, bring up their children in China until they had reached an advanced age, and then apply for them to come here. I do not think that is what we want to have happen in this country. We want immigrants to come here as families and bring up their children in this country from the earliest age possible, so that, when they grow up, they will really be Canadians. It is for that reason this rule was made. It was made of general application because there was a considerable number of cases where, in our experience, we found there was no desire to apply for the wife, often no desire to apply for the daughters, but only for the sons. It is not true that we insist that any of the children come with the mother. The wife can be applied for alone and the children can come subsequently in any order as long as they are admissible.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Yes.
If the father is living in Canada and the mother has passed away, will the children come then?
Oh yes, we do not insist on the resurrection of the mother.
Some of the conditions you impose are almost as difficult.

The hon. member for Vancouver East did refer to a number of sad cases. I admit that there are some cases which, on the face of them, look very difficult. There is one thing about which I should like to remind the committee, and that is that we can only have so many people in our office in Hong Kong. We have to send highly trained people there if they are to do the work at all efficiently. The working conditions are frightful and the amount of work, the pressures and difficulties are much greater than in any other immigration office anywhere in the world. Every time we spend two or three days of the time of the officers in Hong Kong dealing with one of these hard cases, we are holding up 10 or 12 applications of equally worthy people who, in most cases, would be readily admissible. That is the
[Mr. Pickersgill.1

real explanation as to why we often appear to be hard hearted; because we do know from our experience in the administration that every time we have to take infinite pains with one of these difficult cases about which we have genuine doubts we are holding up the other work of the office in Hong Kong.
One might ask why we bother to take these pains. The hon. member for Nanaimo thinks security screening is totally unnecessary but I do not. The fact is there are no vital statistics in China that we can rely on. We do know there is a great deal of fraud practised in some of these cases and the hon. member for Vancouver East himself said yesterday that, in some of these cases, these people were simply using Canada as an avenue to the United States and although I cannot cite a single case I am afraid that has sometimes been true.
Others do that, too.

Others do it too; that is quite right. We try to stop it in every case but it is extremely difficult to stop it in these cases because we do not have access to the kind of records that are available to us in practically every other country from which we receive immigrants.
For all these reasons, I have come to the conclusion that, as from today, no further new requests will be entertained for the review of a Chinese case in which there has already been one review made by the department after the original rejection. No further requests will be entertained for the review of a case in which there has already been one review made by the department after the original rejection.

I think it is terrible. That kind of decision will create more difficulties than can be imagined.
