The reason for taking this position, which I have considered with great care, is that these prolonged and very expensive reviews of cases which have already been carefully reviewed, some of them four or five times, occupy the time of the officials who would otherwise be engaged in dealing with current applications, and thereby cause unnecessary delays in dealing with the applications which come to the department from day to day, and which, in most cases, are much more deserving of consideration than those which have already been considered.
With, as I say, the limited staff which is all we are justified in having at Hong Kong, it is just not possible to have these repeated reviews of old cases and keep up with the current volume of work.
There is one other aspect of this matter of Chinese immigration about which I also want to say something. Hon. members and particularly those from British Columbia but from other parts of the country as well will have received, as I have, a great many representations about certain changes it was felt would be desirable in the regulations with respect to the admission of Chinese.
One of them, which the hon. member for Vancouver East referred to yesterday, I must say on the face of it appears very absurd, and that is the requirement that Chinese Canadian citizens go to Hong Kong and spend a great deal of money in order to get married and bring their wives back here when, if they did not have to make that expense, they could use the money for other purposes such as getting established.
As I say, on the face of it, it seems quite absurd that there should be any such regulation at all. It is not applied generally to immigrants from other countries but there are reasons which I think are known quite well to those hon. members who have had much to do with these cases which make this an extremely difficult problem. However, I have consulted my colleagues about this and I have received their approval to announce today that as an experiment the department will authorize the entry to Canada of fiancees of Canadian citizens of Chinese origin.
Would the minister speak more slowly, please. I am endeavouring to record his words.

The department will authorize the entry to Canada of fiancees of Canadian citizens of Chinese origin, under the following conditions.
They will be examined at Hong Kong as though they were immigrants. If they are found to meet the immigration requirements
they will be given a Canadian non-immigration visa, provided they are in possession of a travel document authorizing their re-entry to Hong Kong.
The marriage will have to take place within 30 days after the arrival of the fiancee and the marriage will have to be performed according to Canadian law. Upon production of a marriage certificate issued by the appropriate provincial authorities an order in council will be passed authorizing the fiancee's landing, and landing will be granted.
That is a big improvement.

The third condition is that the applicant in Canada will have to make a cash deposit of $1,000 at the time of the application and this deposit will be returned to the applicant after the marriage has taken place or in a case where it is evident that the fiancee cannot be admitted to Canada as not meeting the usual requirements-that is to say that when the examination is made entry is refused for medical or other reasons

the money will be returned. In any case where the marriage does not take place within 30 days after the arrival of the fiancee in Canada, the cash deposit will be forfeited and the fiancee will be deported.
While this procedure seems very stringent it will, I think, be quite possible for every bona fide applicant to comply with it, because the cash deposit and the cost of the transportation are about equal. In fact, I think it would cost more than $1,000 for the return passage to Hong Kong and therefore the question of putting up that amount of cash as a deposit will not be any serious impediment.
I do think this is a humane way of dealing with a very difficult problem. If hon. members felt they had to insist I could give reasons why we have to take the kind of precautions we do, but I would prefer not to do so.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say to the minister that the latter part of what he has said is strict but it certainly is an improvement and I am certain it will be welcomed by all of us and by the Chinese Canadian citizens who are looking forward to marriage.
I do not wish to take up the time of the house unduly but I do want to say most definitely that if I had not heard from the lips of a cabinet minister, let alone the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, the statement about the closure of Chinese immigration cases after certain procedures I would not have believed that such a course of action could be possible.

If you have not sufficient staff, you should get more staff; if you have not the trained staff you should train the number required. Why throw completely overboard every principle of British justice for the reasons outlined?
I think this is one of the most disgusting and disgraceful policies ever laid down in this parliament. Mr. Chairman, I find it difficult to comment in parliamentary language upon the decision just announced by the minister with respect to Chinese immigrant cases generally.
It does not apply to cases generally.

Those cases which have been reviewed once. I find it difficult to appreciate just what this government thinks it is trying to do when it announces a decision of this kind at this stage in the session after having delayed the estimates of this important department until this time. was done deliberately in order that the estimates of this department would not receive adequate discussion and examination.

Will the minister then say

We have been urging upon the minister a simple change in the administrative policy or practice, call it what you will, of his department which would remove all these objections. That change is that where an applicant is rejected the reasons should be stated in full and the applicant should be informed and should be given an opportunity to indicate whether he wishes his sponsor iri Canada informed of the reasons so that his case can be heard in Canada and an opportunity be given to meet the objections or grounds upon which the department has based its adverse decision. It is extraordinary, sir, how, when it suits the department or the minister to raise difficulties on that ground, it does so by saying that the information is confidential or that the question of security is involved. But when it does not suit them,

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration when they find themselves in difficulty, then the confidential nature of the grounds upon which the rejection is based vanishes out the window and there is the widest publicity given to the reasons for the rejection or order for deportation, whatever it may be.

Sir, this is another outrageous misrepresentation. The department always gives reasons and is obliged by law to give reasons for deportations. They should not be confused with rejections. We do give reasons for deportations.

Does the minister not recall the Brent case in which the courts of this country, from the Supreme Court of Ontario to the Supreme Court of Canada, held that the department had not given reasons and that they had given the person concerned no adequate opportunity to meet the case against her? Does the minister not recall the Spalding case in which the courts of British Columbia found the same thing?
I have heard of both of them, yes.

In that case there was an admission by counsel for the appellant, which was the crown in that instance, that the hearing before the special inquiry immigration officer was conducted in violation of the essentials of justice. These are the findings of the courts whom the minister professes to respect, but when we confront him with them what does he say? He says there are no rights attached to immigration cases or he says-
To immigration.

-in direct contradiction of what the courts have said that they do the very things that the courts have found they do not do, namely, make full and complete disclosure of the case against the applicant or the person ordered to be deported, as the case may be.
There is all the difference in the world between the two.

As I say, when it suits the department to say that they will not reveal this information because it is confidential or because there is a matter of security involved then it is not revealed but when they find themselves in trouble these principles go out the window and there is the widest disclosure of the grounds in an attempt at self-justification on the part of the minister.
I refer to two cases which have come before the house. The first one I am going to refer to is the case of Paul Robeson. We are told, sir, that particularly where a man is rejected or excluded on the ground that he is a communist there must be the most complete secrecy maintained as to the grounds of the


department's decision and the surrounding circumstances. When Paul Robeson was excluded and the subject matter was raised in the house, what did the minister say? Not only did he say that Paul Robeson was excluded because he was a known communist, which may or may not be the case, but there was no secrecy there. The house and the country were informed of the opinion of the government with regard to this man's political affiliations. Not only that, but the minister went on to say with respect to Robeson, as found at page 2821 of Hansard of April 11:
. . . who was coming here to perform under what were, according to the information I have, communist auspices.
Where is the security there? Gone out the window. The widest possible publicity was given to the fact that the department has knowledge not only of his political affiliations but the political affiliations of the sponsoring organization.
The facts were known by everybody.
Yet we are told in other cases when we try to find out why a person is excluded that the reasons cannot be revealed because to do so might compromise our security arrangements.
The facts were notorious.
Oh, so it is to be in the discretion of the department whether or not the facts are notorious.
If they are notorious, how can you keep them secret?

It is to be in the discretion of the department to brand one man as a communist and an organization as communist although no court has so found. The minister is going to blacken the reputation of these people by saying that the department knows them all to be communist. What kind of principle is that?
I thought the hon. gentleman agreed with my decision in that case.

We are told in other cases that the reason why this information cannot be revealed is that it may be embarrassing to the applicant to have it made public, that this, of course, would be bad, and that we cannot even inform any other individual, even the sponsor in Canada, of the reasons for exclusion even in cases where there are not security grounds because it might embarrass the applicant. But when the minister is embarrassed and it suits him and his departmental purposes to make the information public, in an attempt to blacken the reputation of the person concerned, there is no

hesitation in saying just why they were ordered deported, as in the case of Mrs. Spalding, which was discussed here previously.
On March 14 I asked for some factual information as to whether she had been excluded; whether she had had to post a cash bond and so on; was the deportation order subsequently quashed in the supreme court; did the Department of Citizenship and Immigration then appeal; has the time for appeal to the supreme court expired; has the department yet refunded the $1,000 and so on. I did not ask for the reasons, as I might well have done. There was no suggestion in any of the questions as to the reason why the order was made, because I did not think the information would be given. The minister has told us time and time again, when we have urged him to give the information, that it cannot be given because it is confidential. But in this case where he found himself in an embarrassing position and when apparently his only defence was to smear the reputation of the lady in question, he gave every last bit of information as to the reasons why she was excluded, including the amount of money she had with her, the number of children, and an allegation with regard to her domestic relations, not one bit of which information had been asked for. The minister has played ducks and drakes with his own policy that information cannot and will not be revealed because it is confidential. Without rehearsing the details of the case, I might just say that the major grounds upon which that order was made were subsequently found to be the dark imagination of the department itself and not to be justified in fact.
What we have said is that some order must be brought out of this chaos which the department has made of its treatment of immigration applications. There is a very simple way of doing that, namely by following the ordinary principles of justice. Where the application is rejected the department should state the reasons and give the applicant and/or his sponsors in Canada an ormortunity to meet the reasons and to argue against them. It should set up a proper appeal and review procedure so that the merits of the case might be tried with a minimum of delay, with the certainly that the merits in fact were being dealt with and that the applicant was not groping around in the dark, not knowing what case it was he or she was obliged to meet.
Recognizing for the sake of argument that there is some validity in the position taken that information given by an applicant should not be made public we were prepared to go
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration along with the minister and to suggest that it be not made available to anybody without the consent of the applicant. It is a very simple thing to provide for that. The applicant gets a notice that his application is rejected. It could be done by a short addition to the letter, at the bottom of the standard form, reading somewhat to this effect: "The reasons for the rejection are the following." Then the reasons would be particularized. Then you could go on to say this: "If you wish to appeal this rejection, you have the right to do so; and if, in order to facilitate your appeal, you wish to inform your sponsor in Canada and have him instruct counsel, if he wishes so to do, would you please indicate by signing here." Then if the applicant wished to reveal the reasons, he would say so. Then this endless business of correspondence back and forth with the minister about which he has been talking and the endless reviews by individuals would be ended because the case could be argued and decided with finality. The applicant and his sponsor would know what were the reasons for the rejection and they would be able to meet that case on its merits, with appropriate counsel to assist and to protect the interests of the applicant and the sponsor.
Until some such simple procedure is adopted-whether it be with respect to Chinese immigration cases or with respect to cases of immigrants from any other part of the world-you are not going to resolve the chaos into which this matter has fallen. With all the earnestness at my command I argue that such a procedure, far from increasing the burden of administrative work, would lessen it immeasurably because you could build up a body of precedents and get the merits of the cases disposed of at once, instead of each case being decided upon a principle which rests somewhere in the mind of the minister and no one knowing from time to time what principle is applicable to what case.
The act of the matter is, Mr. Chairman, that the bar association has made recommendations to this effect and others which would produce order out of this chaos. Last year, when we had the matter up for discussion, the minister sought to dismiss the bar association recommendations on the ground that they were made in one case for political purposes and in another case by a disgruntled lawyer. But it is strange to be obliged to report that the bar association enlarged this committee, had them make a further study, and had as chairman of that committee a gentleman whom I doubt whether the minister would describe as disgruntled, unqualified or even politically unsuitable.

No; he is a most distinguished gentleman.

That committee came to almost identical conclusions and made recommendations which were the same as the preliminary recommendations and conclusions arrived at by the committee of the previous year and which the minister was characterizing by the language that I have described. Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a question. Is there any limit to the number of Chinese that can come to Canada? Mr. Chairman, I think this has been a most unfortunate speech that the minister has made today. I am sure that it would not have been made two months ago.
I have been waiting for two months to make it.
Why was it that your colleagues agreed to it only today?

I am sure the minister could have had it before the house earlier. 1 am sure that the minister will be forced by public opinion to repudiate the statement he has made today. The hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon. member for Kamloops have advanced arguments as to why a statement of this sort should not be permitted to stand unchallenged in any free parliament anywhere. The hon. member for Nanaimo this morning referred to the treatment we are extending to people from India and to people from members of our own commonwealth. We must not lose sight of the fact that the people of China and of India are watching what we are doing in connection with the handling of these immigration problems. I for one am ashamed of the policies we have carried out in Canada,

particularly over the last 50 years, in connection with Chinese who wish to come to Canada.
I am sure the members of every political party will agree with me that, on the whole, the Chinese have been very good citizens. It should be recalled that for 25 long years we had a barrier which permitted less than a dozen Chinese people to take up residence in Canada. Then, when we were fighting for the survival of democracy we made some concessions and we allowed some Chinese to enter. For the minister to say now that he is too busy to take the time to review some of these cases that are still pending must not be allowed to go unchallenged.
That is not, of course, what the minister said.

That is the logical conclusion from what he said, that he is going to say no all along the line and not let them in.
I have a case which goes back for many years, and there has been a great deal of correspondence in connection with it. I re-jsent very much the suggestion that the minister has thrown out that these people are a nuisance. Charlie Quan has been one of my best friends for 25 years. Let me review very briefly a few of the details in connection with Charlie's life. At 13 years of age Charlie left his home to go out and earn his living. He received the magnificent sum of $4 per month in Singapore. As a result of faithful service he had his wages increased to $6 per month at the end of the first year; then, $8 at the end of the next year; then $10 and then $12. After seven years he had been able to send home to his parents something like $200. Eventually, he was able to go into debt and raise the $500 a head tax to come to Canada. He left his wife in China and his first son was born after Charlie arrived here. In due course, he went back to China and another son was born. After seven years in Canada he went back to China again and a third son was born. Then, the depression came and Charlie did not get back home again. The father never saw the third child who died when he was about 13 years of age.
During the Japanese-Chinese war the parents of two children lost their lives and the Quans adopted these two children. They had no intention of coming to Canada. As a matter of fact Charlie had sold his Canadian interests and fully intended to go back to China to spend the rest of his life. In the meantime, his elder son had become a civil engineer and he came to Canada to take his master's degree at the University of Toronto. When the change in government came in China the preference was to stay in Canada.

The department has been good enough to make it possible for the young chap to take up residence in Canada. There has been a great deal of correspondence about this unusual case.
Now that Charlie's wife is in Canada the daughter, who was married of course, is barred from this country. These two adopted children, who are still in their teens, are also barred from Canada. The minister says that this sort of case cannot be considered because there would be a great many other similar cases. I think it is unfortunate that 15 million people are trying to hold this northern portion of this continent where I am sure 30 million people could live much better than the 15 million, but of course I do not expect the minister of immigration to solve all these problems.

Perhaps I could just ask the hon. gentleman a question. He is not, in this case, complaining about the administration. He is complaining about the regulations, is he not? Under the present regulations these children are not admissible. If the regulations were changed, their applications would naturally be considered.
The minister says it is too much bother, and there has been a lot of correspondence in connection with this particular case.

No, sir, I think in fairness the hon. gentleman will admit that these two adopted children are not admissible under the present law; that is the law as it is now. If the hon. gentleman is asking that the law be changed, that is one thing; but surely he is not going to complain that it is poor administration on my part to obey the law.

Oh, no; I have had correspondence in connection with a great many other Chinese cases. Like other hon. members, I am sure that we are rather cautious about how critical we are of the minister because some of these cases that have been turned down by the officials are given sympathetic consideration by the minister and previous decisions are reversed. For the sake of future cases one might have to bring before the minister-

I had not intended to take up any of the time of the house in speaking on these estimates, but I think possibly I can make my remarks in two or three minutes: instead of taking 15 or 20. I am perhaps

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration fortunate in not having many cases of East Indians in my constituency, neither do I have many cases dealing with Chinese or Japanese immigrants. We have a great many immigrants coming from Europe to the rich farming section which I represent. A year ago I had the opportunity of being in Europe and I visited the homes of the relatives and friends of a great many people who have come to our country from Belgium, Holland, France and Germany. I would like to bring this to the minister's attention. I am particularly pleased with the type of immigrant he has brought to the county of Wellington in the province of Ontario. When I visited the homes of these people I learned that those who had emigrated from those countries are the best ambassadors Canada has in those countries.
In case after case the immigrants who had moved to Canada were writing letters home to their friends and relations telling them what a wonderful country Canada is. This caused me to think back to some 11 years before when I was in Europe with the army of invasion. It occurred to me that it would have been wonderful if we had had these same people in those countries at that time.
I would hope that whatever he does in his department the minister will continue to do the good job he has done in the past and will continue to see that we bring to Canada the type of people who will appreciate the opportunities presented to them here and who will not hesitate to write home to their friends and relations advising them that Canada is a great country and that they have good friends and neighbours in Canada; in brief, that it is a nice place to live in.
Every place where I visited the relations of immigrants in Europe, and I visited a great many, I found that we had a warm bond of friendship and I do not believe such a bond between two countries could be achieved in any other way.
I would like to commend the minister for the good job his officials have done in seeing to it that we bring to Canada the best kind of immigrants from the continent of Europe. In my constituency there are not many immigrants from the continent of Asia so I am unable to comment on that situation. I do find, however, that the Department of Citizenship and Immigration has done a great service for Canada in the good relations it has created between the European countries and the citizens of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, may I take this opportunity of thanking the minister for the many courtesies he has extended and the attention he has devoted to the cases which
[Mr. Hosking.l

I have brought to his notice in the past. Some of these were extremely difficult and I want him to know that I do appreciate his efforts in this regard.
Having said that, it is quite obvious that my remarks are not intended to be a criticism of personalities nor are they intended to be what we have heard this afternoon, unfair criticism. Rather, they are directed to a much more important matter, namely a policy which will reverse the present trend where we are having very few people enter this country.
There are several matters which come under the jurisdiction of the minister and his department in which I am interested, and immigration is certainly one of them. I believe that the Department of Citizenship and Immigration is one of the most important departments of government because of the fact that it deals with people who will work and produce and increase the assets of Canada.
May I remind the minister there is a limit to our growth unless we increase our population. All the available statistics point to a very sad development because they reveal that over the past few years we have had a marked decrease in the number of people who have been allowed to come to Canada. There is no doubt about the fact that the policy seems to be restrictive rather than liberal.
I know there is an argument that the increased prosperity in Europe has resulted in a reduction in the number of people who are willing to come to Canada, but I personally know of several cases in which the procrastination and delay in the department reaching a decision has caused frustration and resulted in the applicant and his family succumbing to a sense of futility and abandoning all hope of coming to Canada, and therefore they have sought entry elsewhere.
I am not advocating a wide open door policy; certainly no one in his right senses would do that. I do think, however, we should humanize our policies somewhat and show a little more tolerance. I do not hesitate to express appreciation for the immigrant because I think his record is excellent, and what Canadian does not have such ancestry? Everywhere we look we see these people, their energies and talents absorbed with our own in building a greater community and a richer country.
It has been my experience that behind the word immigrant is always a story of characteristics that we Canadians appreciate-courage, love of freedom and a very deep devotion to this country which these people have selected voluntarily as their

own. It seems to me there are perhaps many people in Europe who should be given the opportunity of coming to this country. Let me remind the minister that there are still over 414,000 refugees from captive nations in Europe under the care of United Nations refugee commission. Surely amongst those are many worthy cases that ought to be permitted to enter Canada.
May I just point out to the minister that one of the best ways for us to safeguard our freedom is to allow a generous number of people to come to this country who have not been enjoying freedom. They are the element that does not take freedom for granted.
It seems to me that as long as our country is one in which there are vast uninhabited spaces and as long as we have a productive capacity that calls for an ever-increasing per capita consumption, unless we are able to increase our population by natural means to a proper level the question of immigration will always hold our attention.
We should have a sound aggressive immigration policy especially at a prosperous time such as this. That policy must be based on selective immigration and yet it must also be human and tolerant. I think the situation is well described in an editorial which appears in the Montreal Gazette of May 29, 1956:
The fundamental fact of life for Canadians . . . is the necessity of expanding our population as quickly as possible, in order to reduce the heavy financial burden which we now pay for the privilege of remaining Canadians. The imposts borne by every Canadian to meet the handicaps imposed on us by limited consumers, small industries, overwhelming communication problems, outside defence commitments and severe climatic limitations are too obvious to need elaboration. If we are to remain a nation, rather than to become a forty-ninth state, we must have more people and as quickly as possible.

Mr. Chairman, I want to assure the minister before I start that I am not going to be critical of him. He and I have had differences of opinion before and I want to assure the committee that he came around to my way of thinking before we got through and so we got along all right.
I would like at this time to direct a question to the minister. Does the minister or the government have any preference as to the number of immigrants admitted into Canada of different nationalities? Would the minister answer that question before I proceed?

Perhaps while I am on my feet, sir, I may be permitted to say a word about what the hon. member for Edmonton East said concerning refugee camps. I was
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration very much impressed by some of the representations made to me by the Ukrainian Canadian committee about a year ago urging that we go through the refugee camps and take a second look. I think perhaps the hon. members knows, and perhaps even wanted me to say, that we sent a mission including a distinguished member of the citizenship branch of my department who is of Ukrainian origin, and one of the officers of the immigration branch, to take a second look at all the camps. We think we are going to find quite a number of eligible people in the camps.
There are certain other liberalizations we think we can make, particularly in co-operation with the provincial governments. One difficulty we do have is that if we bring people to this country who cannot satisfy all the health requirements and they subsequently have to have treatment or welfare assistance; that is not a charge upon the federal government, in most cases it is a charge on the provincial or local authorities. We do not feel that we should create potential problems for them without their concurrence in our doing so, but we are taking the most liberal view we can.
The hon. member for Huron asked me a question which I think I could best answer by reading a few sentences from what Mr. Mackenzie King said in 1947 which is still the fundamental policy of this government.
Did you write it?

I think you might say that it has been our policy to give the most encouragement to immigration from countries like the United Kingdom which have institutions similar to our own. That is not because we consider there is any inherent superiority in those people over other people, but because immigration is the process of tearing people up by the roots and trying to transplant them. As the hon. member who is a farmer knows, it is easier to transplant into soil which is similar to that from which you take the plant. It is for that reason that, generally speaking, our immigration promotion policy is confined to Europe and to some degree to the United States. I sometimes think that we ought to look for more immigrants from the United States, but I think the debate on another subject last evening has shown how frightfully difficult it is for a relatively small country like Canada, small in resources by comparison, to make much impact, publicity-wise, upon a country like the United States.
Our general view is that, other things being equal, it is better to get immigrants from
7220	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration countries that have our constitutional, parliamentary, democratic and free type of government; that they adapt themselves more easily and more readily.
Why it it we get so many more immigrants of one nationality than of another? Are those immigrants picked by application, or how are they picked?

Many of us might like to have it that way, but you cannot conscript immigrants. They volunteer to come and we do our best to encourage the people we want to come. The people in some countries are much more ready to come than those in other countries. I am very pleased, and here I am constrained to say, although it pains me to do so, that the hon. member for Kamloops was right and I was not entirely right last year about the assisted passage loans; I think there is no doubt that, by accepting the advice of the hon. member for Kamloops and a lot of other persons inside and outside the house, and extending these loans to cover dependents as well as the breadwinner, we have increased immigration from the United Kingdom. I just made a quick calculation when the hon. member was speaking yesterday and the increase in the first six months this year over last year is about 11,500, and of that number 7,000 are from the United Kingdom. I do not think that asssisted passage is the main factor, but I think it has been a contributing factor. I think better publicity has been another factor.
In this respect I cannot compliment the hon. gentleman. There was a lot of talk on the other side of the house in January and February of 1955 about the great unemployment crisis. We have absolute proof that that did discourage immigration, particularly from the United Kingdom. This year, while there were nearly as many people on the unemployment insurance rolls, we did not have a debate in the house. There was a more hopeful attitude here which was reflected in the figures. So far as the situation in Europe is concerned, they have had the same kind of full employment in both years.
I am quite discouraged about the decline in immigration from The Netherlands. There are varied reasons for this, the most important of course being the full employment they have there. There is no doubt that the immediate cash advantage of having your passage paid to Australia-it is free there and they do not have to pay it back-does appeal to a certain number of people. Why do we not do that? I think the answer is very simple. The passage to Australia costs a great deal, and so does the return passage. The passage to Canada costs very little. With the buoyant employment we have in this


country it is very easy for a person to earn his passage back. I would be very much afraid that if we undertook to pay passages we would find we were providing some relatively cheap holidays for a lot of people. It is a problem, but I think we ought to be realistic about it. We did try it in the 1920's and had that experience.

Immigrants are brought here when there are not jobs waiting for them when they get to Canada, nor do they have assurance they will get jobs, but I have received representations on behalf of certain people who had jobs promised to them here and yet they had difficulty getting in. As long as a person has complied with the regulations he should not have too much trouble when he is assured of a job before he leaves home, much more so than one who comes here with the idea that he can get a job. I think the minister should take that into consideration when he gets applications from people who have relatives here or who know people who can offer them jobs before they leave home. Such people are not going to become a charge on the state and they should be given preference.

We do our best, but sometimes there are personal factors that make a case very difficult. In this context I may say that the problem of security screening is a most difficult one. Except for the hon. member for Nanaimo I do not think there are many who think it can be dispensed with. It does create great difficulty. I do not say it is responsible for all delays, and I certainly do not blame anyone for them. This is the kind of operation that can be carried on only by trained people or it would be a travesty. It is a real problem.

Mr. Chairman, from what we have heard in this debate on immigration and in other debates on immigration I think most hon. members will agree that there are few departments of government that command the direct human touch more than immigration. We in Canada have always considered family life and close family ties as being one of our great assets. Therefore I cannot accept the statements that we have heard this afternoon that any action by our minister would at any time interfere with the cementing of family ties. Such a statement is most unreasonable and there is no justification for it in the face of the experience I myself have had.
As hon. members know, I also represent a constituency in which there are countless families whose homes have been destroyed and whose members have been forcibly

separated, and these people have been prevented from cementing their ties with their families. In every case that came to my attention affecting the reunion of a family, although the minister has not always been able to yield to the human request, he has wherever possible and on every occasion made the cementing of human ties and the bringing together of families who are separated a basic principle of life in Canada, and certainly he has granted those requests on every possible and conceivable occasion.
It is therefore very difficult for anyone sitting on this side of the house to hear members of the opposition take isolated individual cases, notwithstanding the minister's clear-cut explanation that where the department is satisfied and convinced that the facts are as represented, the department would grant those applications. We have a minister and we have departmental officials who have their jobs to do. If they were to make mistakes and admit people into this country who should not be admitted, the opposition would be the first to criticize them.
I am satisfied that, especially where the question of family ties are concerned the minister and his officials in every part of the world will most certainly yield to the requests that families be brought together again. I can only say that I have considered the minister's actions and found them to meet the situation. He tempers the cold wording of the law with a very warm, human and almost paternal consideration, and in doing so he certainly is administering the law not only in conformity with its letter but certainly with the spirit of our Canadian way of life.
While I am on my feet may I draw to the minister's attention the fact that because of our expanding economy and because of our industrial development we can look back now for about ten years and find that the more than one million immigrants who have entered Canada since the war have certainly been helpful in our expanding economy. We are still growing; there is still room for improvement, and certainly we shall require additional manpower.
In that respect I should like to draw to the minister's attention the fact that there is perhaps another opportunity now, because I think most of our sources of immigration are almost dried up, in the Europeans who have immigrated to North Africa and who because of developments in the past two or three years, are now almost compelled to flee from North Africa. Perhaps here is a fine opportunity for us to be alerted to the fact that there are thousands of highly [DOT]desirable immigrants who may now be willing
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration to come to Canada. I suggest to the minister that we alert our officials in Paris and Rome and in other European centres to that fact and to encourage as much as possible the immigration of such people from North Africa. They are mostly affluent and intelligent people, Europeans who had to flee Europe during the war holocaust and who are now also unfortunately fleeing North Africa because of the very dangerous situation there. I think from that source we can now obtain a number of fine immigrants who can continue to assist the economy of Canada in the same way as the more than one million we have brought to this country since the war.

I was interested in one comment the minister made regarding the Australian policy, in which he said that Australia pays the passage and does not require repayment. May I ask him whether that applies to all immigrants or merely to those from the United Kingdom? In the light of the figures I have seen, which I put on the record yesterday, which indicate that in 1955 Australia received 54,000 persons from Europe under the resettlement scheme-
I think that originally was only for immigrants from the United Kingdom, but the Australian policy has been expanded far beyond that.

While fully appreciative of the dangers of even a loan scheme, let alone an outright payment of passage scheme, I would urge that the department have another look at this question and possibly have a modified scheme between an outright payment and a loan-perhaps a long-term loan would be the answer-because the figures seem to indicate that Australia is benefiting from the availability of refugees-
It is not just regular; it is European immigrants generally.

Well, from European immigration as a whole, more than Canada is. In view of the real need for population, about which there is at least no division of opinion between us, perhaps, one could categorize it as a highly competitive business of encouraging immigrants to come here. If Australia is succeeding to a greater proportionate extent than we are should we not, then, have a fresh look at our own competitive position and see what we can do to improve it visa-vis Australia; not only to beat out Australia -that would be a foolish thing to rest it o" exclusively-but to look at it from the viewpoint of our own proper self interest and the responsibility that we have to those who require new homes?

I do not think we really want to engage in competition with Australia, and I do not think the hon. member really suggests that. I think what we ought to try to do is increase the total numbers. The Australians need immigrants very badly. In some ways they need them worse than we do because of their isolated position in the world, and it has never been part of our policy to compete actively with them.
When we come to the supplementary estimates it will be found that there are several ways in which we are attempting to do something to encourage people. I might say in passing that it is perhaps not top well known, though we try to make it known in Europe, that any immigrant who borrows money to come to Canada and undertakes to go on a farm has his loan cancelled at the end of a year if he stays for a year on a farm. We make that special inducement in the case of farm labourers. We also now extend the loans beyond the two-year period in cases of need, now that we have taken dependants.
Perhaps in some ways the most useful thing of all that we have done is to establish the new family assistance program. There was a distinct feeling on the part of many immigrants that it was rather unfair that, in the year when they first came here, and perhaps needed money more than they would ever need it again, they were ineligible for family allowances. The payment is the same as the minimum amount of family allowances. It has been very well received. The payments are now being made, since July 1, I think, under the principle on which we operate, that once an estimate is brought into the house where the government has a reasonable majority we can sometimes anticipate approval. I hope no exception will be taken to that.
Not in the present circumstances.

I should like to add a word or two to what has already been said about the problems of immigration. First of all, so far as any problems I have taken to the minister are concerned, he has looked after them personally and I wish to thank him for that.
I want to say a word or two about what the hon. member for Cartier had to say about reuniting families who have been separated through difficulties of war or other causes, and his view that where it is at all possible to reunite them in Canada that should be done. I think that should1 meet with the approval of the minister and Canadians generally. In that connection I should also like to refer to the requests of Chinese for the admission to Canada of their families. I have a good many friends among the Chinese 

people in the city of London. We find that they are very law-abiding and that very seldom, if ever, are they involved in infringements of the law. They have never been known to be on relief. Most of them are self-employed and engaged in business. Consequently I hope that a humane approach will be the policy of the department with regard to their interest in bringing members of their families to Canada.
There is another point I might mention along that line. Many Chinese families probably will never have the opportunity to be reunited with their relatives in Canada because of the communists taking over the mainland of China; therefore that reduces the possible immigrants to a very small number. The hon. member for Kamloops mentioned the recommendations of the Canadian Bar Association. I think they should be very seriously considered, because these men have made a very thorough and complete study of the problems.
There is another matter I hear discussed in my part of the country. People wonder why it is that so many immigrants are attracted to Australia and New Zealand as compared to Canada. I am also wondering what efforts are made to attract citizens of the United States to become Canadians. There is no doubt that many of them are becoming interested in our great natural resources. That is quite evident. But when they become interested I should like to see them come to Canada and become Canadian citizens, and not remain in the United States and reap the benefit of our resources. I think a judicious plan of advertising to attract the right type of people might be advantageous as far as we are concerned.
Then there is another question that is always in people's minds. It has been mentioned a good many times to me and I am going to give two cases that were brought to my attention. One was the case of a young English chap and his wife who decided to leave the British Isles and were going to shop around before they decided whether to go to Australia, New Zealand or Canada. Their first call was at Canada House. The officials there were interested, but they said that there were a great number of applications, that the bookings on the various steamship lines were full, and that possibly they would have to wait a couple of years before they could come to Canada. They were very disappointed.
The minister knows as well as I do that when you come out of the door of Canada House on Cockspur street you look across the street and see the offices of the Canadian Pacific Railway. They decided to go over

to the Canadian Pacific and see what they had to say. They told them that they wanted to come to Canada but that they understood that space was at a premium and difficult to obtain. They wanted to know what they could expect. The officer of the Canadian Pacific Railway said, "Would two weeks be soon enough?" Yet they were told across the street in our offices in Canada House that they could not expect to get passage within a couple of years.
Then there is the case of another chap

and I know these people-who went there and told the commissionaire on duty at the door that he was interested in coming to Canada. As a matter of fact, on his first trip he did not even get past the commissionaire.
Is the hon. gentleman quite sure he is right about his facts? I do not think the immigration office is in Canada House at all.
He went to Canada House and that is what he was told. When he came out the door he went right across the street to the Canadian Pacific Railway office.
Blame the Secretary of State for External Affairs!

I can give the minister the names of these immigrants if I so choose. If they had not gone across the street to the Canadian Pacific Railway the chances are that they would have gone to Australia or New Zealand. We do not know what goes on in our offices abroad, and there is a lot of doubt in people's minds as to what does go on. When these two cases were brought to my attention I began to wonder myself. I think it is time that we took a look at the situation. I do not think the people of Ontario are too happy about the management of the department or the policy of the government as far as immigration is concerned.

If I may just say a word or two, I gave some misinformation a moment ago to the hon. member for Kamloops. I have looked up the matter and I find that the part of the loan to farm labourers that is cancelled is inland transportation in Canada, not sea passage.

I should like to ask the minister about the liaison between the dominion and the provinces in connection with the attraction of immigration from abroad. I have here in my hand two articles. One is from the Globe and Mail of May 12, 1956. It is headed "54 Per Cent of Immigrants Ontario-Bound". The article gives statistics which justify the headline and indicates that of that number the great majority remain in Ontario. I have another article from the


Globe and Mail of April 24, 1956, which reproduces an editorial from the Vancouver Sun entitled "Go After Immigrants". I shall read some extracts from it:
British Columbia needs its own official immigration policy.
Labour minister Lyle Wicks, back from an Ottawa conference on immigration, said he was troubled because B.C. faces "a critical labour shortage this year".
He skirted around the obvious solution without touching it.
Then the article goes on to say this:
Then he said-
That is Mr. Wicks.
*-B.C. wants its share to help with "the essential program we have on the way".
"Unfortunately," he added, "most of our new citizens seem to stay in the east."
Then the editorial continues:
This is true. There are job opportunities in the east. There are also job opportunities in bustling: B.C.
But the east is nearer to Europe. After reaching: Ontario the immigrant may be baffled by the 2,000 miles of journey between him and British Columbia.
Another reason why Ontario gets the big bulk. of immigrants is that Ontario goes after them. It has organized its own immigration. Alberta did the same on a smaller scale.
Then it continues, and this is reprinted from the Vancouver Sun, as I said earlier:
Long ago the Sun urged the B.C. coalition government to do something similar.
The implication of the editorial, of course, is that the British Columbia government has-not taken the necessary steps. What I want to ask is this. We know that Ontario maintains-I believe I am correct in saying this

an immigration office in its provincial offices in London, in Ontario House. From personal knowledge I could not say whether or not British Columbia does the same thing at British Columbia House. While I am not trying to criticize the minister in the dominion government if any province is not doing what it should or could do in order to encourage immigrants to settle in that province, still there is a real problem, I know, with regard to the geographical distribution of immigrants when they come to Canada.
While I am sure the minister will say- and I would agree with him-that we cannot regiment them, that this is a free country and that we cannot compel them, except to a very limited extent by assisted loan passages and so on, to remain in a certain area or indefinitely in a certain type of work and that they will go where the attraction is the greatest, I feel that, whether it be a provincial responsibility or in part a dominion responsibility, an effort should be made

to acquaint immigrants with the opportunities that would confront them in all parts of Canada.
Certainly the opportunities in British Columbia are second to none. I would say they are the greatest anywhere. What degree of co-operation exists between this department and such provincial agencies as there are overseas, and what effort is made by the dominion government to do that which I have suggested, namely to make it as easy for immigrants to get to British Columbia as to get to Ontario or other parts of eastern Canada?

As the hon. gentleman has suggested, Mr. Chairman, this is a real problem. I have the impression, however, that the attractiveness of British Columbia, both from the point of view of wages and climate-
And the class of people you meet out there also.

And general articulateness is such that they have fairly well overcome any geographical handicap they might suffer. Every time I go to the prairies I find that the great complaint is that when we do manage to get some immigrants to go to the prairies, once the first cold day comes along they are on the train on their way to British Columbia. In spite of the editorial in the Vancouver Sun, which I had already read, I do not think British Columbia has come off badly at all in the post-war immigration.
There is no doubt that there are a great many areas besides Ontario and British Columbia to which, perhaps because economic opportunities have not been so insistent, it has been more difficult to interest immigrants in going. We do, of course, make certain provision for inland transportation for certain kinds of immigrants as far as Winnipeg, in order to try to equalize the flow. But as far as our offices here know about them, we do try to indicate the opportunities in all the provinces and to do it quite fairly.
As far as co-operation abroad is concerned, we are trying to keep the closest possible contact with every provincial government that has any representatives abroad. To this conference that Mr. Wicks was at, and which was referred to in the editorial, we invited representatives of all the provincial governments, and we have done everything we could do to encourage them to help us in every way possible with this problem. Immigration is, of course, a matter of concurrent jurisdiction, under the constitution. I had a meeting some months ago with the minister responsible in Toronto. We have always had the most cordial co-operation 67509-4594

I am not going to ask the
minister to pass any judgment as between the efforts being made by the provinces, because I imagine he is in enough trouble without getting into trouble of that kind as well. But it is striking when one realizes that 54 per cent of the immigrants go to Ontario.
I would think that 54 per cent of them stay in Ontario.
Yes.

But we estimate-this is just a guess and nothing more, though we shall know more after we get the census figures for this year-that at least 20 per cent more immigrants find their way eventually to British Columbia than go there in the first place.
They are intelligent immigrants.

As the hon. member knows -and that is reflected even in the membership in this house-there is an enormous immigration into British Columbia from other parts of Canada. Indeed, I am the only member of my own family who does not live in British Columbia.
I do not want to make any comment on whether or not he would be a desirable immigrant into British Columbia, but I am sure the minister is welcome any time he cares to come out and settle there.
I might mention that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam invited me to go there to run against him. I did not accept his invitation, but I reciprocated it.

Naturally, coming from British Columbia as I do, I am delighted to hear that people from other parts of Canada want to come there. However, I do not see why our immigration should be at the expense of any other part of the country. I should like to be sure that proper efforts are made so that immigrants will be directed initially to those parts of Canada where employment opportunities exist. I hope that will be done.
There is one other related problem upon which I should like a report from the minister, and that concerns the shortage of farm labour in British Columbia. I find that during the course of one of the minister's speeches, oddly enough in the course of a speech delivered in Edmonton in November, 1955, on the future of the Canadian Indians, the minister said:
As minister of immigration, I know we face a long-term shortage of farm labour in Canada,

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration which we have been trying to meet through immigration, but which is becoming increasingly difficult to satisfy with newcomers from abroad.
I should like him to say a word on that. I took it up with him by correspondence recently in connection with the situation in the farming area of my constituency. I should like to know specifically what is being done to meet the problem through overseas recruitment. Perhaps the minister would say a word also regarding the assistance which is paid in connection with the long rail journey in Canada itself.

I am afraid, sir, that this is an economic question. We have tried one source after another of potential immigrants for farm labour, but as hon. members who are farmers know, the competition for labour in this country in recent years has been very acute. As we do not impose any restrictions upon the immigrants, our experience has been that they tend to leave the farms and go into other employment. We do, of course, provide this rail assistance as far as Winnipeg in the hope of distributing them more evenly throughout the country. The debt is cancelled if they stay on the farm for a year, but it has not proved to be much of an inducement. It is, I am afraid, a really appallingly difficult problem.
I do think there may be some possibility-[DOT] we tried this year but we started a little too late, and we are working on it-of encouraging some of the German farmers who have crossed from East Germany into West Germany to come to Canada. Since all the land is taken up in West Germany they cannot go into agriculture there and we are encouraging them to come to Canada for a year or two as farm labourers with the view eventually to becoming farmers. They were mostly people who were substantial at home and of course would not contemplate a career as farm labourers. This may help to alleviate the situation for a while.
I am very hopeful, and here I am putting in a plug for another branch of the department, that by the training courses which we have started on the prairies for Indians and which I hope to see extended across the country, we can encourage an increasing number of young Indians to be interested in farm labour with a view eventually to some of them becoming farmers. This wo uiu pe a transitional stage from the more primitive life they live to life in our more urban society.
The farm labour problem is a difficult one, and I do not think we are going to find any solution to it through immigration, though

The minister says that he and his administration are not responsible for the consequences of these particular actions and that of course is as far as the minister can be compelled to answer; but I do not think the hon. member is out of order in drawing to the attention of the committee at this time deaths or other occurrences which take place on Indian reserves when we are discussing the administration of the Indian affairs branch.
I can only repeat that the minister has stated he has no responsibility, and he cannot be compelled to answer further than that. However, I cannot at the moment rule out of order a discussion of the situation that has arisen and which I take it the hon. member is indicating in his opinion is a matter for which the department should accept some responsibility.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I certainly feel this does not fall under the jurisdiction of the provincial administration, on the reservation at Brantford. The federal department maintains justice on reservations and the provincial department has absolutely nothing to do with the administration of Indian reservations.
I think it is time that something was done about non-Indian indigents living on Indian reservations. If the department is not prepared to provide these people with a decent burial if they happen to die on a reservation, I am wondering if the department considers that these people are supposed to crawl off the reservation before they die.
I fail to understand why payment should not be made in this case, because it has been made before. The undertaker gave this service in good faith and had no idea that the


expenses would not be paid. When he presented a bill for two funerals he was advised that the bills would not be paid. If the undertaker had been advised that his expenses would not be met he could then have chosen to perform the burials and taken his chances on collecting his expenses, but he was not so advised.
I think the minister should stretch a point and undertake to see that the present bill is settled, then advise the undertaker that such expenses would not be met in the future. Because of the correspondence he has had with the departmental officials in this regard the undertaker is aware of the department's attitude concerning payment and will be able to govern himself accordingly in the future. I do not know what the minister is going to do if some day he receives a phone call and is advised that a non-Indian indigent had died on a reservation and the people there are wondering what to do with the corpse. If this occurs he will have another problem on his hands.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to take a few minutes in which to draw the attention of the minister to what I consider unnecessary delay and red tape in settling Indian affairs; particularly estates, which sometimes run on for years, and rental leases and so on.
The worst case of delay in my riding concerns an irrigation canal which was built through the Indian reserve in 1919. I have in my hand the file which I received a month ago containing correspondence between the Indian affairs branch and the provincial and federal governments concerning the case I have in mind. I intend to quote briefly from these letters in order to give the whole picture of this scheme that was commenced 37 years ago. In this instance the Indians were to benefit as a result of the sale of certain land, but to this day they have not received a penny.
I might point out that under the project I am discussing the water conveyed through the ditch on Indian land has built up flourishing communities such as Oliver and Osoyoos, which are located in that area. The ditch was put in to provide water under an irrigation scheme for veterans after the first war, and millions of dollars have been added to our national wealth through the use of this water and the development of this land.
As I said, I intend to quote briefly from these letters in order to sketch in the background for the minister, because he may not be aware of it. I have in my hand a letter dated June 19, 1919, addressed to Hon. Arthur Meighen, minister of the interior at Ottawa, part of which reads as follows:

I understand that the inspector of agencies at Vernon is to make a report at once, and thereafter, I presume, you will be able to give us your decision without delay.
This is with reference to the transfer of Indian lands to the provincial government. I continue:
We have made you an offer of $10,000 for the tract in question, but I suppose, if the locusts are as bad as your dominion entomologist reports, that this would be a high figure.
I go on to another letter in that year addressed to Mr. Pattullo by Mr. Meighen which refers to the letter of June 19, and which he states has not been replied to. It reads in part:
I might say that the deputy superintendent general of Indian affairs informs me that he, during last month, asked our inspector to make an immediate report as to the advisability of making portions of the Indian reserve south of Okanagan lake available for returned soldiers and he hopes to have a reply very shortly.
Then the next one is dated July 23, 1919 from the minister of mines.

Unless the hon. gentleman wants to put this on the record, may I say that I have seen this correspondence and I agree that the matter ought to be straightened out. I agree thoroughly with the hon. gentleman and we are trying to do it.

The minister has indicated that he is aware of it. It is a disgraceful way to treat Indians, to make them wait 37 years for money which was promised them in 1919. Nothing has been done, and the latest letter of January 5 of this year, addressed to the deputy minister of lands and forests at Victoria by the Indian commissioner for British Columbia reads:
I wish to acknowledge with thanks your letter of December 22, and copies of an exchange of correspondence with Chief Manuel Louie. I have requested our superintendent at Vernon to assure Mr. Louie that our negotiations with you are proceeding satisfactorily and that there is no need for further correspondence on his part.
It started 37 years ago. Here is another letter addressed to the assistant to the deputy minister of lands and forests by the Indian commissioner for British Columbia under date of February 29, 1956:
I am wondering if any progress has been made with regard to the above since your letter of January 31.
This matter has, as you know, been outstanding for many years and I am afraid that if a settlement is not effected at an early date the Indians concerned may change their minds, leaving the problem still with us.
The whole file is of the same nature. Personally I feel that the department has been absolutely incompetent in dealing with the Indians. The original price was $10,000, and then the land area was cut down. The
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Indians now demand $7,500. Although the land has become very valuable the provincial government offered only $5 per acre with 25 cents severance allowance. I think it is time these Indians were given the full protection of the department in order that they may collect what I consider to be a fair and just demand, that is roughly $7,500. Actually that is only interest on the original $10,000 which was offered to them 37 years ago. I hope the minister without any delay will see that some action, legal or otherwise, is taken to obtain this money for the Indians. I let it rest at that because the more I read the more disgusted I become with the conduct of the department.

Since this matter has been drawn to my attention I have been pressing to have it settled. While the hon. member was speaking I received a note to the effect that the commissioner of Indian affairs has just been advised that a meeting has been called for August 14 with the minister of agriculture in Victoria to bring this matter to a conclusion. I hope sincerely it is brought to a conclusion. I do not know whether it is possible for us to take legal action in the matter, as I am not a lawyer and therefore would not be able to say, but certainly I can assure the hon. gentleman that we will push hard to get this thing settled both quickly and satisfactorily.

I want to point out that I am not blaming the present government in Victoria, as I do not think it is their fault. This matter has recently been drawn to their attention. I do blame this government for being slack.

Perhaps I should reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Roberval on the immigration item.
(Translation):
Following my visit to the Pointe-Bleue reservation, last June, I instructed the officials of the Indian affairs branch to complete their survey on the school situation and the condition of the road as quickly as possible.
Hear, hear.
I understand that a report will shortly be submitted.

Thank you very much.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member who has just spoken referred to a matter in connection with Indians which has remained unsettled for 37 years. The matter I have in mind is not that old, although it has been before the department for the last two years. There have been conflicting statements about the present position.

The hon. member for Yorkton has had a question on the order paper in regard to the Caughnawaga Indians, in which he asks for information from the St. Lawrence seaway authority and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. At one time we had a statement from the minister that everything was all right, that everything was in order; on the other hand we had a statement from the reserve stating that the Indians are not satisfied. Then we had a statement by the chairman of the St. Lawrence seaway authority that everything was fine, that they were paying for the land owned by the Indians and they were happy about it. Then about a week or so ago we saw a band of Indians in full ceremonial dress up here to interview the minister and everything is supposed to be all right.
I do not know whether it has been done deliberately, but this information has not been brought down although the notice has been on the order paper for three months. There is still no satisfactory statement about it, and I wonder if the minister could tell us what the situation is in regard to the land taken from the Caughnawaga Indians.

Mr. Chairman, I would be pleased to give a summary of the matter. When it was determined that the route of the St. Lawrence seaway would be such that it would be necessary to take some land from the Caughnawaga reserve, the normal procedure in ordinary circumstances would have been to apply to the band council of the reserve and attempt to get an understanding about the surrender of the land. That is what we would do in Ontario or any province west of Ontario.
Under the law as it was decided by the privy council, if there is to be a surrender of Indian lands in the province of Quebec, or in certain other provinces east of Quebec, the residual right of the province comes into play. Therefore it was impossible to proceed in the way in which we proceeded on the Blood Indian reserve, when land was required a few months ago for a canal across that reserve. It was impossible to proceed in that way; therefore it was necessary for this parliament to give the St. Lawrence seaway authority power under its act to expropriate.
Such expropriation would, of course, extinguish all rights, the right of the federal crown as trustee for the Indians, the right of individual Indians, and whatever residual right the province may have. At the time this was done a meeting was held with the then council of the band of the Caughnawaga Indians. It was explained to them what would be required, and a committee was set


up by that council to discuss with the representatives of my department all the problems that would arise in providing individual compensation to individual holders.
In addition to that, of course, it was my view and it is still my view that, over and above compensating individual Indians for their individual holdings, there should be some compensation to the whole band for having this canal in front of the reserve. In other words, an Indian reserve cannot be treated like other property; there is a communal interest as well as series of individual interests. The way this was carried out was that the St. Lawrence seaway authority made an over-all offer to me in my capacity as superintendent general of Indian affairs and representative of the crown in this context, and I said I could not accept any offer finally until I had first reached an understanding with the individual holders, because I felt that the St. Lawrence seaway authority must pay the full cost of the compensation and that we must not have to come back to this parliament for a vote to provide for a residual amount. Therefore it was impossible for me to make a final settlement with the seaway until settlements had been made with the Indians individually and collectively.
We have set about making these individual settlements and a considerable number of them have been made. In the middle of that process, some weeks ago, an election was held. Most of the councillors were defeated, and a new council was elected. The new council came here accompanied by legal advisors and had an interview with me. If I remember rightly, they were elected on July 4, and they had an interview with me some little time after that. At that interview they made a number of representations. The first was, of course, that the reserve was inviolable and that it was not competent for this parliament or for anybody else to take any part of it. I said that was a point on which I just could not agree with them; that there had been no challenge to the validity of the legislation passed by this parliament; that I could not admit that the reserve was inviolable; and that if they felt as a council that they wanted to challenge this legislation they would have to challenge it in the courts.
I suggested to them that I did not think we could stop history and that I was quite sure the seaway was going to be built. I also suggested very strongly that I believed very firmly that when this canal is completed and all the work is done the reserve will be in a much better state than it is at the present time. I have repeatedly given assurances in the house, and I repeat them now with the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
full authority of all my colleagues, that if after the negotiations are completed or fail to be completed with individual holders there is any individual who does not feel that the offer he has been given is adequate, the case will be referred to the exchequer court-I do not think it could be taken in the ordinary course to the exchequer court but it will be referred to it-and the value determined in that way. These negotiations are still proceeding, and the last report I had was that settlements were still being made.
I have every reason for believing-in fact, I believe very strongly-that these are thoroughly adequate settlements, and I would not agree to them if they were not. I also feel that it is very important to get certain advantages for the band as a whole. I am carrying on discussions with the St. Lawrence seaway authority, which are not completed, in that regard. One of the things they are doing that is going to add very considerably to the value of the reserve is that there are a number of swamps virtually in the village, and these swamps are being filled in at no cost to the Indians and made useful land for building purposes. The shore, in many ways, is going to be improved. There is going to be an area where the Indians will have access to the river, where there will be a beach and some other amenities.
I admit that people, whether they are Indians or not, do not like to be disturbed. They do not like to have their homes taken and have these changes made. That is true not only of the Indians of Caughnawaga; that has been the experience of the Ontario government, I believe, in places nearer than that. But I think all of us realize that some of these things have to be done. The important thing is that there should be full and complete compensation given to the Indians for everything that is done to their detriment.
The seaway authority is making provision for water intakes and sewer outlets from the canal. There is no proper water or sewage system in the village at the present time, and I certainly am very hopeful that I can persuade the council of the band that it would be desirable to have that kind of improvement. Of course it is not going to be forced upon them.
On one point I believe it is not possible to meet them at all, and that is on the doctrine of inviolability.
In any case most of the land has already been taken, so the only thing that could result, if they should challenge the legislation at this late date and be successful, would be to get damages or have the seaway diverted to another place. I do not think
any of us would believe that is very reasonable, and I hope that as time goes on the Indians themselves will feel that this is not a reasonable attitude and that it is not constitutionally correct, as I do not think it is.
I do not know whether I have answered all the hon. gentleman's questions, but if there are any more I should be glad to try.

The minister spoke a minute ago about the Indians' claim of inviolability of their property. Probably the approach has not been right, as far as the Indians are concerned. He made the statement that you cannot stop the progress of history; but, at the same time, neither can you blot out the past history that belongs to that particular piece of property. I do not think the band is objecting too much to having their property taken away from them. One can understand, as the minister has stated, that no one likes to be moved off his property, but consider the history of this land. It is a property which goes back to the time of His Christian Majesty of France in 1680. They did not like the land allotted to them as a reserve because it was not arable land, and they were then granted this piece of land by His Christian Majesty. The Jesuit fathers of a later day claimed the land was granted to them, and it ended up with a proclamation by General Gage awarding the land to the Caughnawaga Indians. All this is history having a particular bearing on the land they own. Whether it was under a French king or under an English king the land still remained crown property to which the Indians have a right that has been given to them by treaty and as the minister said, it has not been surrendered.
It cannot be surrendered.
It can only be surrendered to the crown.

No, it cannot. Perhaps I did not make myself clear. If the reserve had been in Ontario instead of Quebec the Indian band could have surrendered the property for sale to the St. Lawrence seaway authority in return for a consideration, but because it is in Quebec, if the Indians surrender it then it reverts to the provincial crown. That is why there had to be special legislation passed by parliament to enable it to be expropriated. They can make a surrender but they can only make a surrender to the province. That is the situation.

What I am trying to bring to the attention of the house is that it has been the history of the Indians down through the years that everyone who has dealt with them has always ended up by giving them the
