Supply-Citizenship and Immigration wrong kind of deal. They have always received the short end, and it is natural that down through the years the Indians have become suspicious. You cannot blame them for that. I might read from the royal proclamation of 1763. I shall not read the first part but just the last:
And whereas great frauds and abuses have been committed in purchasing lands of the Indians to the great dissatisfaction of said Indians; in order, therefore, to prevent such irregularities for the future and to the end that the Indians may be convinced of our justice, and determined to remove all reasonable cause of discontent . . .
Even though this statement by His Britannic Majesty is nearly two centuries old its effect should be observed today. When the matter was before the house last year I think the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace asked a question of the Minister of Transport with regard to the expropriation. I did not think "expropriation" was the right word. It was a case of them being compelled to give up the land, because after all the riparian rights to the land still belong to the crown irrespective of who owns the land. But the minister stated that while the lands were being expropriated they were only going to be used for the time being, until the seaway was in operation, and that they would then be returned. Then he paused and went on to say that did not necessarily mean to say they would be returned to the Indians. To whom are they going to be returned? Are they going to be put up for sale or transferred to the provincial authority for highways, or what is going to be done?
The point I am trying to get before the house is that in dealing with the Indians they should be entitled to the same kind of deal as a white man. The white man would be holding out for the highest price. Is it not the duty of the Indian affairs branch in looking after the interests of the Indians of the Caughnawaga reserve to hold out for the best deal they can get, and to see that the Indians get a square deal for a change? In land transactions today real estate operators are making fortunes in buying and selling property. In this case the Indian has inherited land which has come down to him through generations. He is proud of it and wants to remain there. He does not want to be removed. If he is going to be removed he would like a little more land added to his reserve to compensate for what is taken away. Surely he is entitled to get the very best price for it.
The matter of the crown is not in question. It is just a matter of how these Indians have been treated. The Caughnawagas are part of -the Mohawk nation. They belong to the old


Iroquois confederacy that gave yeoman service to the British crown and the French crown. This particular branch, the Caughnawaga tribe, did not give allegiance to the British crown but gave their allegiance to the French crown. Because of their allegiance to the French crown and their particular case I think they are entitled to a little more consideration than other Indians who surrendered their reserve lands in the past.

I should like to say one very brief word. I quite agree with the hon. gentleman that the Indians are entitled to more consideration than white people. So far as the individual property is concerned, I do not think the particular Indian is entitled to any better deal than any other Canadian citizen with similar property, but because they live on a reserve I think the band is entitled to some consideration as well, and that is precisely what they are getting here.
It so happens that I went to Caughnawaga myself one Monday and I happened to buy a Gazette in the central station, Montreal, before I went to the reserve. I read in it a letter from one of the people who lived just outside the reserve complaining about the deal he had got from the St. Lawrence seaway authority, and he said, "I do not want a million for my property; I just want to be treated as well as the Indians."

With regard to my motion for the production of papers, I would agree with the minister in this respect, that the Indians do require special attention. They are not like ordinary citizens who can go and obtain property in other places. Reserves were set aside for these people by treaties. Many of the treaties are 50 or 100 years old or even more.
I think those treaties should be honoured. The right of the Indians to maintain and defend the rights granted to them under the treaties should be honoured. Since the Indians are looked upon as the responsibility of the department, I think the department should undertake to see that the rights of the Indians are maintained; and if access to the courts is not available then it is the department's duty to see that these rights are maintained. The only difficulty, of course, would be that the department would be hiring counsel to fight a case against another branch of the government.
I do think that the matter of the treaties and the rights of the Indians under those treaties should be thoroughly settled, and the band should be informed of their position. What bothers these people is that they feel they have certain treaty rights, and there is no one there to tell them what rights they

are and where they stand with regard to them at the present time. In many cases they do not understand. I also agree with the minister that because the St. Lawrence seaway development has necessitated the taking of some 1,200 acres from the reserve the settlement should be a proper and just one, and in this case I think the Indians are entitled to just a little more than the people in the surrounding districts because of the special circumstances under which the Indians live.
I think it is a wise thing to see that the band gets an extra grant. Does the band get an extra grant as a band for the expropriation of the 1,200 acres, or is a portion deducted from what each individual receives?

I can answer that very easily. We are attempting to make settlements for individual holders that are just as good as the settlements for individual holders off the reserve. Nothing whatever is deducted from what they get. In addition, the band is to get a substantial amount.
That grant comes from the seaway corporation?

Yes. The seaway has to pay the whole shot. After the new band council came to see me in the parliament buildings some time in July I spoke to Mr. Chevrier. I said, "They have a new council, and there are some of these people who do not really understand what has gone on in the past. They question whether you have not taken more land than you really need, and they also resent some of the surveyors who have been on the reserve because they claim they were not properly authorized." There were several complaints of that sort. I said, "Would you go down yourself and meet with the band council and take your best engineer with you and explain why you need all this land, what it is for and what you are proposing to do?"
Mr. Chevrier went there on the first day on which he and the band could agree, which I think was about four days later, and he spent the whole evening there. The director of Indian affairs went with him. I have every reason to believe from the reports that have reached me, that a good deal of the misunderstanding was removed on that occasion. One thing is that a certain amount of this land was taken for temporary installations while the canal is being built, but when construction is completed that land is going to be cleared and given back to the Indians in a better state than it is now. Another thing which apparently they had not all understood is that several swamps right on the edge of the village are going to be
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration filled, in order to make good building land. I think the hon. member has been to Caugh-nawaga and knows of the topography there. When this whole operation is completed I feel that not only will there be generous compensation but that the village and the reserve will be a better place for Indians, and that is what ought to be.

I agree with the minister in that. I would suggest to the minister that had he done that in the first place; had he given the Indians some explanation of what was going on and if a better explanation had been given by the authorities, we would have avoided a great deal of misunderstanding and trouble, and certainly a great deal in the way of hard feelings. The fact is that these people felt they were being imposed upon, that somebody was imposing his will upon them. That was a bad thing for their morale.
The incident that brought the matter to our attention was the fact that here was a proposition that had been carried on, a big construction project, and before any settlement was made some of the Indians found big drag line and excavation machinery in the backyard toppling over their homes. No settlement had been made. Scarcely any efforts had been made. I think it was a case of maladministration. I believe a little bit of foresight might have prevented much of the bad feeling and misunderstanding which was created.
I still think the department would do a great service to the Indian people if they would go to such bands, go with them over the original treaty, give them explanations, let them know what are their rights and where they stand, and recognize their rights. If they wish to appeal to the courts and take their case there, I think the right of access to the courts should not be denied them.
The other thing I wanted to mention was this. Suppose an individual Indian was given some kind of offer for his land. From some of the reports I have received rather unofficially, they were sort of like scribblings on a piece of paper that had no final standing whatsoever. Where an Indian was given to understand that a certain amount of money was to be made available to him for his property and he was not satisfied with it, to whom should he appeal? I understand that you had representatives of your department who were on the reserve throughout the whole matter. But the Indians found that the same people were on the appeal committee as were on the committee that was making the original offer. I refer to your departmental representatives. The result was that the Indians felt that

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration they were making an appeal to persons who were interested in the first place in making the offer.
As to the settlement of such cases, I do not know how many cases there are going to be where people are not going to be satisfied with the settlement. I was glad to know that after some negotiation, where these people did not wish to make a settlement for the amount of the offer an opportunity was given to them to receive an advance so they could settle in some other homes when it was possible for them to do that. I think on the whole a great deal of misunderstanding could have been avoided if the Indians had been taken into the confidence of the department, of the departmental officials and of the seaway authorities. Wild stories were going around. They were wondering what kind of a deal they were getting, and there seemed to be no one to whom they could appeal for any element of justice. They were not told what the deal was. They were not told who this authority was. They were wondering whether somebody was just moving in on them. Not knowing what the situation was they were naturally afraid that they were going to be exploited.
We are going to be following the settlement of the whole matter, and we shall see that justice is done. But the position the Indians themselves are in is a natural one. They feel resentment. First of all they feel incompetent to deal with the situation, and they feel that there is no one to whom they can appeal for justice. They feel that the departmental officials are biased in favour of the government and of the authorities. I think that is what has caused a great deal of the trouble. If returns had been made in the house and if the Indians had been given the necessary explanation, I think it would have helped a great deal to straighten out the matter.

I should like to say just a word about that matter. No doubt we made the great mistake of consulting the government of the band and not the opposition. But there was consultation from the very first day with the seaway authorities. Mr. Chevrier himself went there in the very early stages. There has been complete consultation with the duly elected authorities throughout. But what happened was that there were two parties on the reserve. In July there was an election and the opposition got in.
That will happen here next time.
Don't be so optimistic.

As soon as that happened and as soon as it was indicated to me that the new band council wanted to see me, I saw them at once. I listened to everything they had to say; and I may say that I went a great deal longer without my lunch then than I did today in order to do that. In the end I think the Indians were at least satisfied that they had been given a decent hearing. I arranged this meeting with Mr. Chevrier. We intend, of course, as is the right thing to do, to deal in the same way with the new council as we did with the old one. I do not know how else you can carry on this consultation except with those who are elected by the band. Things will probably be better now that there has been a recent election.
I do not think it is fair to the officials who have been carrying on this work, or to Mr. Chevrier and the seaway authorities to give the impression that there was not consultation. The fact is that there has been the fullest consultation at every stage. It so happens that there are many people who have property at Caughnawaga who do not live there but who live in other parts of Canada or even in the United States, who may not have been fully informed because they were not at home when these consultations took place, and who may have had reason to feel that they were not informed. However, the information was given through the regularly constituted authorities.

Does not the genesis of the trouble lie in the individual deals that were made, or the first offers that were made to members of the band? Was it not in the fact that some Indians sold at a rather low price for their property; other Indians waited for five or six months, and got a much better price than the one they were originally offered for the sale of their land? Was that not the cause of most of the trouble?
No, I do not think so.

This is the administration item of the Indian affairs branch. It is not my intention at this time to go too much into the administration of the whole set-up. However, there is one matter in which I am particularly interested and I think it is fundamental to the establishment of these people as Canadians and their integration as part of the Canadian people.
I refer to the matter of the education of the Indians. I have the departmental report before me. I might say that the situation now is a great improvement over what it was 10 or 15 years ago, having regard to the

standard of education. The number of students receiving high school education has greatly improved. The record, however, is still fairly bad looking.
I see that, as may be found at page 76 of the departmental report, the number of students is given in the various provinces. In British Columbia, with about 31,000 of Indian population, you have about 175 students in high school or taking high school courses, and that is at any rate a great improvement. In Alberta, with 15,000 there are about 70; in Saskatchewan, with 18,000, about 77; in Manitoba, with 19,000, about 78; Ontario with about 37,000 of Indian population, about 200; and Quebec, with 17,000, about 15 attending high school.
I was wondering what the departmental policy is with regard to continuation schools and the education of Indians there. Is the department still carrying on the schools under the inspection, let us say, of the provincial government?
Yes.
Is there any move under way or any intention to take any part of this work and try to make arrangements or provision for them to provide the facilities? Has the government in mind any change?
I should be glad to make a brief statement on this subject.
I think it would be very helpful.
I do not want to be the one to raise points of order on the minister's estimates, but I had hoped to have something to say on education.
Perhaps I should delay that until we get to the education item.
I do not want to be critical, but perhaps my hon. friend might wait until the education item.
If the minister will make a statement on that item, it will be all right.
I shall be glad to.

Before we leave entirely the item which covers the St. Lawrence seaway and the treatment of these Indians, I wonder if the minister has given any thought to the possibility of acquiring 1200 acres somewhere else which the Indians could have to look upon as theirs, so it could be said that none of their original holding had been taken from them. I have spoken several times on this matter in the house and I have discussed the matter with the minister, who has, I must say, always been extremely sympathetic and ready to do anything that could be done.

I gathered from him on one occasion that he saw numerous practical difficulties in the way of obtaining the land, but I think it is a fundamental principle that reservations should be held inviolate. If there are occasions like this one on which it becomes necessary during the development of the country that some of this land should be taken, then an equal amount of land, of equal value and in just as good a location, should be acquired somewhere and given to the Indians to make up for the land which has been taken away. My feeling is that whether or not the Indians of this generation wish to dispose of the reserve, it is our duty and responsibility to those who will come in the future, 75 or 100 years from now, to see that the reservation is held inviolate for the descendants of those people who are now on the reserves. Would the minister make a comment on that?

I would be pleased to, sir. We did consider that very carefully and it would not, of course, be possible to duplicate the land. We would have to take some other land somewhere else. It just so happens that a large part of the reserve is unoccupied and has always been unoccupied. It is our feeling we should consult the council of the band, and if necessary the band itself, because my own opinion would be that the money would be better spent in improving what they now have and making some of that land more valuable and more productive rather than in extending the amount of land.
I know the hon. gentleman is thinking of Alberta and of some of the things we have done there where the Indians are engaged more in rural pursuits. The acquisition of more land is often very important. However, these Indians on the Caughnawaga reserve are not engaged in agriculture to any considerable extent. My feeling is, subject to their views of course, that the money could be better spent in improving what they have rather than in getting more acres, but we intend to consult them about it.

Could the minister tell us why it is that this land on the Caughnawaga reserve has not been used by the Indians? Is it because the land is not suitable for agriculture, or because it is heavily forested, or is there any other particular reason?

I suppose it is part of that urbanization that is characteristic of this whole continent, and perhaps of the whole western world. Apparently these Indians can climb to dizzy heights that I could never hope to reach, and make a great deal more money than they could by cultivating their acres.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration

The reason I bring the matter up, Mr. Chairman is that it was impressed upon me when we were in the Indian affairs committee that there is a constant temptation on the part of certain Indians to acquire a piece of land of their own and to seek to dispose of that land to advantage to a white man. There is an incessant pressure upon the part of the white man exerted upon almost every reserve to get into that reserve and get a piece of land and make it the land of the white man. I think that is all to the bad. While we are in a sort of process of flux, changing from one type of life to another, I think we must be exceedingly careful that nothing of that sort takes place on any reserve.

Item agreed to.
Welfare of Indians
73. Operation and maintenance, $2,638,947.

I have just a few remarks on item 73. The question of our treatment of the Canadian Indian is one in which we are all very interested. I should like to express myself on that point. It seems that the attitude of the public and their concern is insufficiently reflected in the administration of the affairs of the Canadian Indian. This item gives us an opportunity to express ourselves, to point out ways and means of improving the plight of the Canadian Indian and giving him a better deal than he is apparently now receiving.
This is not a political matter. In the last little while we have heard various speakers call for more honourable dealings with the Indians. I especially admired those speeches that were made by various members who are close to the problem, in which they tried to bring out the facts as they really are. In the main it is a rather sad story, and I think one that should give the white man a guilty conscience. We print statistics, write articles and give lectures on our accomplishments so far as the Indians are concerned. It seems to me that as legislators we should not be satisfied with our past accomplishments until such time as the health, sanitation, opportunities for local self government and self determination of the Indian is more equal to those enjoyed by the white people of this country. The Canadian public know that is not the case today, and they insist that we do something about it, because it is a matter of concern to everyone who values social justice and recognizes that we do have responsibilities to these people.
Let us look into this a little deeper. Over the years we have spent millions in order to build up the economies of other countries. During the past five years we have spent over $128 million on the Colombo plan. Just


a few days ago we voted another $34,400,000 for that same plan. In addition, since the war we have spent over $4 billion to help the economies of certain countries. Those are fine humanitarian acts, but it seems to me we should follow the moral principle that charity can be exercised better at home through helping these people. I do not understand why we cannot make available to them some of the great surpluses of food and clothing we have in this country. It seems incredible that in a country such as ours, when we are enjoying an unpredecented prosperity, many of the 155,000 Indians in this country do not know what it means to be out of want. The various articles we read in the newspapers draw our attention to the shameful situation.
The minister will recall that last year Jack Deakin wrote a series of articles for the Edmonton Journal which revealed that shameful situation. I should like to read a few comments that are pertinent to this debate.

I do not know whether the hon. gentleman recalls, but I was in Edmonton some time after that and I pointed out that there were some rather serious inaccuracies in those articles. I admit that conditions are not what we would like to see them, but I think the writer of the article, whom I met after that time, himself conceded that some of the things were not quite as they appeared in that article.

I quite appreciate what the minister has said. Nevertheless he will admit that much of what appeared in these articles were facts. This editorial reads:
Canadians are generally aware that this country's treatment of its Indians makes a shabby story. Nevertheless, we imagine that the series of articles by Jack Deakin which the Journal has published in recent days will come as a shock to most of our readers. Mr. Deakin has been visiting the Indian reservations in northwestern Alberta and he reports appalling conditions of hunger, squalor, disease and general misery-far worse than anything to be found in the southern and central parts of the province.
In the more thickly settled areas, conditions on the reservations become widely known, and the various bands have friends to take their part and insist that matters be improved. The northern tribes, on the other hand, are truly "forgotten men". Few know of their plight; outsiders are seldom in a position to help; and so far as the federal Indian affairs department at Ottawa is concerned, indifference seems to reign supreme.
The article continues in this vein:
The miserable state of the northern Indians is often blamed on their own laziness or incompetence, but there is no evidence that this is so. Like many primitive peoples, they have been overwhelmed by changing conditions, with which they cannot cope without help. Their ancestors lived solely by hunting, trapping and fishing, but with the advance of civilization and the depletion of the game, this way of life can no longer support

them. Yet the government, whose wards they are, is doing little to fit them for other methods of gaining a living. Inevitably, we now find them living in the extreme of poverty, in miserable shacks or tents, without adequate clothing or blankets, undernourished, often sick, and in many cases dependent upon a thoroughly inadequate and unbalanced relief ration. The only agency of the federal government which is genuinely helping them is the medical service; but even here its work seems to consist in taking adults and children to hospital, curing them if possible and then sending them back to the conditions which caused the illness in the first place.
It is my feeling that we should approach this matter as one that is deeply human, in addition to recognizing that we have a legal responsibility by reason of the various treaties we have signed with the Indians. I wonder why we should not give them a brand new deal. I suggest to the minister that he prepare an all-embracing program that has been carefully worked out and submit it to the house at the next session, one that will also rewrite some of the game laws which apparently are operating to the disadvantage of the Indian.
As was mentioned by the hon. member for Lethbridge I feel that in any over-all consideration of improving their plight we should certainly retain the reservation as a sanctuary for the Indians. On the basis of some of the information we have received with respect to what is being done on those reservations I am led to say they are nothing more than glorified concentration camps. I urge the minister to make an improvement in their program in order to restore some respect and dignity to these aboriginal people.

77. Administration, operation and maintenance, $9,678,096.

Mr. Chairman, I promised the hon. member for Yorkton that I would say something on item No. 77 about the educational program, and I shall try to make this just as brief as I possibly can.
It has been the view of the department for some time that the best way to educate Indian children is in the same schools with other children, and wherever it is possible to make arrangements with the local or provincial authorities on any reasonable terms that is what we are now trying to do.
The second best way, if the other is not feasible, is to have day schools wherever the Indians live a sedentary life and where the home conditions are such that they will not be deprived thereby of home influence. We also recognize that there are many nomadic Indians in the north and there are a great many cases where there are unsatisfactory
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration homes, broken families or orphans. The residential schools which have done such a magnificent job over the years will, I am sorry to say, likely have a very important role in Indian education for a long time to come.
As I think the committee knows, the Indian population is growing faster than the rest of the Canadian population, though it is not added to by immigration and it is subtracted from by enfranchisement. This increased population is pressing with a severity that increases with the years upon the traditional means of subsistence. It is imperative and urgent that new ways be found for Indians to make a living.
There has been an increasing stress over the past few years and there will be still more stress in the future on vocational education and on ordinary high school education where-ever the pupils are promising. I have persuaded the Minister of Finance quite recently to permit me to establish a system of scholarships for promising young Indians both for high school and university. The present policy in any event is to see that no one is denied the chance to go on to high school if he is properly qualified and the family is willing to have him go. Of course, in the case of self-supporting Indians we do our utmost to encourage them to bear a reasonable share of the cost themselves, but if this is not possible they are not deprived on that account.
I do think this is far and away the most important part of our work in the Indian affairs branch. We have a considerable program for the construction of schools, but we also have a considerable program which is growing every year for capital assistance to ordinary schools within the provinces where Indians are enrolled and for sustaining grants to such schools, in proportion to the number of Indian pupils in those schools. There is no doubt whatsoever about the success of this program wherever it has been tried.

Mr. Chairman, I was very pleased indeed to hear the minister express the views he has just presented in spite of his confession-I think it amounted to a confession, though that is scarcely a fair word because it is not his fault-to the effect that the whole system of Indian education as far as success or failure is concerned has simply broken down, if there was ever anything which could break down.
What I mean to say is that the results have been totally and completely inadequate and the Indian education program has been hodge podge, divided as it is between provincial, local and dominion responsibility, and it has not been fulfilling the role for which it was
7238	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration created. I would warn the minister that some five or six years ago I said in this house almost exactly the same thing he has said, for which I was taken to task by a certain journal in the country and defended by others. I made the terrible mistake in that while I congratulated the residential schools for the fine work they had done in many directions, I went on to say practically the same thing the minister said today to the effect that wherever it is possible it is better to take the school to the Indian than to take the Indian to the school.
My chief reason for saying this is that when a young Indian lad goes to a high school he enters a dream world, a world about which he has heard but which to him has no particular reality. The same is true of the curriculum, which does not permit him to have his education become a reality to him, and he is not able to relate it to the events of his every day life and his habits. The young Indian boy or girl enters his dream world for a year or two and then returns to the conditions which exist on the reserve. These are conditions which I need not describe at this point and which are fully known to the minister and many hon. members of this house, conditions created by economic necessity and by the greed of the white man, who put the Indian on land which would not maintain a gopher. That is so with regard to my own prairie country, and I think the same thing is largely so in the east. There is a situation of unreality. When the young lad or girl goes back to his or her home they meet with the same old conditions, and I am informed that within a month or so or at the most within a year they are back in the social habits that prevail on the reserve.
I certainly hope the minister's ideas will be carried out and that there is a greater contact between the two races. It will have a considerable effect upon the Indians which is not possible when the children are sent away to residential schools, quite often some distance away. When Indian boys and girls go to schools where they can come in contact with other children, with children-we may be right or wrong in this-of what we consider a better type of civilization than that of our red brothers; when they come in contact with these different social habits, that contact is translated into a form of education for those children. In my opinion that is much more valuable than the academic training they may be given.
I could talk on this subject for a long time. For instance, I could talk on the curriculum of the Indian schools and what it should be. I am one who has never admitted that vocational training is in fact actual education. It is true it is part of education, but I have


always refused to see vocational training as education. One of the events of my life was the opportunity I had to study the education of native peoples in Kenya, the Rhodesias and South Africa. I admit I changed my mind somewhat in regard to those primitive people, but that is all. While there I saw the value of vocational training among primitive people.
Wherever possible I am in favour of having the Indian attend the same public school as his white brother, if possible on a mixed basis. In case I should be misunderstood again, may I repeat that I am not detracting in any way from the work done by the residential schools in various parts of the country. But I do suggest that their function today is not as necessary as it was in past days. We have many new media of education in the way of television and radio; we have quicker means of transportation; therefore I do not think the residential school is as necessary today as when it was first originated.
I should like to see the minister get his estimates through, but may I suggest to him that he would have got them through much faster if he had not made such extensive speeches on almost every item. I want to draw his attention to what has been done in northern Saskatchewan in this regard. The minister of education is carrying out some experiments in connection with Indian schools. He has selected young men who are particularly fitted for this type of work. They are paid extra salaries and are sent up into the north where the schools are literally being taken to the Indians rather than the Indians being taken to the schools. We have reason to believe that that experiment is meeting with considerable success.
I shall close by saying that I am delighted to find the minister has the same ideas that I have had for many years in connection with Indian education. I was taken to task for having them some years ago, but I think that was due to misunderstanding and misquotation. I think the minister is on the right track, and I wish him every success.

When item 77 was before the committee I resisted getting into a debate on policy and I am going to try to resist getting into a similar debate on this item, though in view of what has been said on item 77 I must say that I do have definite reservations particularly in connection with this construction item, because in my view there is not sufficient assistance being given to residential

schools in the way of construction. To that extent I must make reservations with regard to the principle enunciated by the minister and other members who have spoken.
While I am not opposed to integrating Indian and white children where possible, I believe that what has happened and will happen to an increasing extent is that there will be a greater emphasis on the building of day schools for Indians, which have a restricted application, with less attention paid to the residential school, which in a vast number of cases is the only school the Indian has an opportunity to attend. What I gather from the minister is that his policy contemplates the eventual extinction of the residential school.
I would not think that would happen for a century.

I am glad to hear that, but I think his policy is to concentrate overmuch on the day school aspect at the expense of the residential school. I submit that we must concentrate to a greater degree on improving the facilities and standards available at the residential schools. Had it not been for the residential schools and the sacrifices of those who started them, there would be no Indian education at all.
I could not agree more completely.

They ran them with practically no support, and now they are being more or less condemned. When compared with the standards at which they should be maintained they are most certainly being abandoned and left in an almost derelict fashion. We should have a sense of proportion in these things, and we should concentrate to an equal degree, if not to a greater degree, on maintaining and improving the facilities at the residential schools and not exclusively on improving the situation with regard to day schools.
There are some questions I should like to ask with regard to the residential schools at Kamloops and at Lytton. There is a big program under way at Williams Lake, and I do not think I have too much criticism to voice in that connection. The residential school at Kamloops is most anxious to extend its high school facilities. That is the only school available to Indians over a very large area. The residential school at Lytton is an old-time school, and it has rendered outstanding service.
That is perfectly true.

They are starved for adequate accommodation. I would ask the minister to
give us some assurance that their needs will be taken care of in the very near future.
Would the minister also give an explanation of the item of $200,000 in the supplementary estimates for operation and maintenance under welfare?
Yes.

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, before the adjournment I promised to deal with a couple of questions asked by the hon. member for Kamloops. One was with relation
7240	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration to our plans for high school facilities at Kamloops. I might say that we have something like $120,000 committed for expansion there. The details of the plan of expansion are being worked out at the present time. At Lytton we are planning to spend about $7,000 for repairs including painting, repairs to the roof and renovating of the plumbing, which I understand is very badly needed.
On the second item, is there anything for provision of new teacher accommodation? That is one of the pressing problems there.
I am afraid my own experience with building would suggest in my mind that you could not build much living accommodation for $7,000, but I shall look into that question.

I should like to say a few
words on this item, because during the discussion of Indian affairs I feel that with respect to education and the facilities that are being provided we have heard quite a bit of some of the problems that exist. In my opinion there are also some fairly bright spots in the country, and as far as I am concerned the program of participation in construction adopted in one area in my constituency is really beginning to show some fruits. I am thinking particularly at the moment of the Alert Bay area, where in my opinion almost a complete transformation is under way.
I might tell the committee that the Indian affairs branch has co-operated with the Alert Bay school board in the construction and operation of a school there which is used both by children of Indian origin and all others in the community. The last figures I noticed showed that the school population was something like 100 Indian children and 80 some odd children of other origins. That does not include the younger Indian children who are in a day school operated by the department. In addition, I think it is interesting to note that the old residential school is being used not for school purposes but for residential purposes for children who come from the smaller reserves somewhat more remote from that centre.
I must say it has been something of a joy to me to see the transformation even in the last 10 or 11 years since I first had the opportunity to see what was taking place with respect to the younger Indian population in that area. There is an almost complete mingling of the various elements of that community. I was particularly interested in the suggestion of the minister, actually on an earlier item, that it is his intention to supplement what is being done in that direction by


increased opportunities for vocational training and for scholarships. I have been somewhat concerned as to what some of these young people were going to find to do in that area. For that reason I am glad the minister has announced that policy and I hope it will be carried into effect as rapidly as feasible.
Until the hon. member for Kamloops mentioned his interest in what was going to be done with respect to a couple of schools in his area I was a little puzzled by his reference to what he claimed, as I understood him, was a disparity between the emphasis being placed on help for residential schools and help for day schools. Actually the amount in the estimates under this item seems to be more or less evenly divided between the two types of Indian schools.
But there are more residential schools, and they have been there longer.

That may be so in some areas, but I felt I should like to take a few minutes to tell the committee that at least in the one area I have mentioned specifically the program the minister was discussing is in my opinion paying off quite well, though it may not be perfect in every detail yet.

What are the general
plans for construction this year? Would the minister say what the plan is for Saskatchewan and how much is going to be spent on the various reserves in the construction of buildings or the building of roads and the like?
This has to do only with schools.

Item 78, and it has to do with education.
As a matter of fact, as it appears in the public accounts it has to do with the construction or acquisition of buildings, works, lands and new equipment. It includes far more than schools.
I think if the hon. gentleman will look at item 74 passed some time ago he will find that refers to other construction.
Oh, yes; that is the earlier one.

take the citizenship items, sir.

59. Citizenship registration branch, $398,265.

Perhaps the minister would indicate whether he would like us to discuss the actual granting of citizenship to prospective citizens under the registration branch or under the citizenship branch proper.
Registration is the proper item, and I should like to boast that we had about five times as many people become citizens in 1955 as in 1954.

Under this item I should like to say first that I think Montreal has been well served in the past year and a half by its new citizenship court. The backlog in that city, which was so very great, has been largely eliminated as a result of the establishment of the court and people seem to get their citizenship papers without much difficulty. However, there are occasions when in dealing with the work of the department, which conducts so much of its operations in camera, unusual situations come to light. Many of these, as was demonstrated in the case of the immigration branch, are matters where somebody cannot get from the department what they want and they therefore begin to complain about it.
It is unusual, however, when we find a situation in which someone has obtained from the department what they want under circumstances which, to say the least, are somewhat peculiar. In a situation like that the person, having obtained her wish, is not going to complain about it. The department is not going to bring in any question of procedure they may have followed previously. The only hope-and it is an unusual one-is where a citizenship application is opposed by someone else, namely by some private citizen. I do not know how often this happens, but it certainly is an unusual situation. That is why a particular case has come to my attention which causes me some little concern because it casts doubt, first of all, upon certain ways the minister has of dealing with things and, second, upon certain of the procedures which are being followed in the citizenship court itself, when a case is opposed.
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
I am going to quote from certain actual court documents in this case, Mr. Chairman. In the very beginning I think the point should be made that the purpose of the citizenship court, the purpose of any such court in Canada, is to act in an advisory capacity to the minister.
The purpose of the citizenship court.

The
purpose of the citizenship court is to act in an advisory capacity to the minister. It is his responsibility to make decisions, as shown in section 10 of the act. Since this case has been fairly widely publicized, we need have no hesitation in naming the individual. It is the case of Madame Giovanna Elisa Feltri-nelli. I give the minister that information now in the beginning, because I know he is familiar with it and I want him to follow my argument.
Why this application for citizenship by Madame Feltrinelli was opposed is of no concern to this house. It is one of those things where there is a possibility of many millions of dollars being at stake. It is a highly complicated matter. Be that as it may, certain people saw fit, within the provisions of the citizenship act, to oppose her application.
On what grounds did they oppose it? They had various grounds, many of them complicated. But I should like to put forward one set of circumstances which they brought to the attention of the court in Canada and which show sometimes just how curious can be the minister's decision.
As we know, the citizenship act in section 10 specifically calls for an applicant to reside continuously in Canada for a period of one year immediately preceding the date of application. Here is the evidence signed by the president of the court of Canadian citizenship. Far from being in Canada during most of this past year, we find that this particular applicant has led a very pleasant life. Actually it is a very pleasant life in Canada too; let me say that at once. But she has led a very pleasant life in other parts of the world. In his reasons for the decision the president of the court of Canadian citizenship says in part:
Has she resided in Canada for at least one year immediately preceding the date of her application, that is from December, 1954 to December, 1955?
She made one trip to Geneva, Switzerland, on January 27, 1955, and one trip to London and Italy in March, 1955. These trips were made by plane from New York. She also made a short trip to New York for a day or so on December 1, 1954, and January 10, 1955.
It is explained that the applicant was obliged to travel extensively both in Switzerland and in Italy by reason of opposant's actions.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration From April 25, 1955, to December 3, 1955, the petitioner lived aboard a yacht owned by the Merida Company, an incorporated company under the laws of the province of Quebec flying British and Canadian merchant marine flags.
I intersperse this remark here in order to point out that that is a seven-month period during which this woman resided on a yacht. Later in the reasons for the decision we find this.
During this period the yacht travelled in the Mediterranean sea where stops-over were made when necessary.
She had to be in Rome and London on the 7th, the 8th, and the 9th of July, in relation to opposant's actions.
From October 3, 1955, to December 16, 1955, the petitioner had to go to New York to consult with her attorneys and on October 28, 1955, she had to be in Rome to see her attorney.
Good heavens, Mr. Chairman, I have gone over this record three or four times and I cannot see where she possibly could have been in Canada at all except when she flew in for a day or two and then went right out to go to Geneva or to Rome or back to her yacht and the Mediterranean.
An itinerant Canadian.

Then, of course, when she had satisfied the requirements of the act, according to the way in which she looked at it, the judge finds as follows:
Since December 16,	1955, that is after the
filing of her petition, the petitioner has mostly lived in Italy to look after proceedings, to make necessary appearances in court.
Then finally the judge of the court says this, and it is interesting in the light of what I have read:
It is the opinion of this court that the absence from Canada during the year preceding the application are sufficiently explained and that, in law, the applicant may be considered as having resided in Canada during the year preceding the date of her application.
What is the name of the judge?
Paul Fontaine is the name of the president of the court of Canadian citizenship.
How did she get her mail?
Which mail?

That is only one of the several reasons why these people felt justified in opposing the application for Canadian citizenship of this particular lady. As I have said, there are a number of other reasons, many of them more complicated and which I am not going to go into at this point. Let us for a moment at this point think how tough it would have been or,
I should say, how tough it is for some people [Mr. Hamilton (Notre Dame de Grace).)
who do not have yachts in the Mediterranean or who do not get over to Rome every two or three months, who cannot fly down to New York to look after some of their business affairs, to get into Canada, and get their citizenship-
It is sometimes tough also for those who have boats.
What is this, the voice of experience?

-and
how easy it seems to be in this particular case, Mr. Chairman. The only person I can think of who got into Canada as easily as this, under somewhat questionable circumstances, seems to be Hal Banks, the vicepresident of the Canadian seamen's union and he was jet propelled by this department as well.
You mean he missed the boat?

When I talk about jet propulsion, that is exactly what happened in this case. We all know that normally there are delays following these applications for hearing, for a week, two weeks or a month. No one expects, of course, to do business on the same day on which the application is made. But Madame Feltrinelli apparently has an inside track. She applied for her naturalization on December 16, 1955 and on March 16, 1956, after a lapse of the statutory minimum of three months to the day, her case was heard by the citizenship court. Perhaps I should congratulate the minister on such marvellous precision, and I would if I thought everybody had obtained the same treatment.
It is not at all unusual in that court.

Unfortunately I know from my personal experience that they do not.
We now come to another interesting point. I do not know whether or not the minister knows this, but he certainly should. According to my understanding these citizenship courts are supposed to be very similar to courts of law. They certainly are not supposed to be star chambers. Yet on the statement of this lady's attorney I am informed that the attorneys opposing this citizenship application were excluded from the courtroom when the case was being heard. To the best of my knowledge if a person is opposing an action in any other court, the person who is opposing has a right to have his attorneys in the court. Here they were specifically excluded. The note I have here is very specific and very clear on that particular point.

There is a sidelight on this. In the course of these star chamber proceedings the court heard certain evidence. When it handed down a written judgment it said, in part, that in the course of her examination the petitioner admitted that she had no permanent residence in the city of Montreal, and that she was actually domiciled at Stanbridge East, Missis-quoi county, province of Quebec. We all know that the citizenship act specifically requires that these proceedings take place in the area where the applicant is domiciled.

Then we come back to Montreal, and part of the process of citizenship is that the person is to take pride in obtaining this citizenship and accept it publicly. These and many other questions enter into this particular situation.
However, Mr. Chairman, two facts which I have put before this committee tonight stand out stark and clear above everything else. One is that here is a person whose application for citizenship was expedited and put through in an almost miraculous way, despite the fact that practically every week of the required period of residence in Canada was spent outside Canada and seven months of it were spent on a yacht in the Mediterranean. The second fact that stands out clearly is that this court in Montreal excluded during the major part of its hearings and during its examination of the applicant the representatives of those who had opposed the application.
The material I have here is also in the minister's file. It has been placed in my hands by the attorney representing those who are opposed to this application. I have given a brief resume of this case to the committee. I conclude, Mr. Chairman, by simply asking these questions. Has this department now reached a stage at which, in addition to all the other things that seem to affect its reasoning, entry into Canada can be facilitated for an individual who is rich and made difficult or impossible for one who is poor? Can the obtaining of citizenship in this country be made a matter of instantaneous decision for one who has enough money to be in a position to spend the better part of a year on a yacht in the Mediterranean and thus establish her requirements for citizenship while, as we know, thousands of people without these monetary advantages wait a matter of weeks or months for this same purpose? And finally, have we reached a point where a minister of the crown in full possession of facts such as these and with a full knowledge of the procedures carried on by the court in Montreal will refuse to intervene and refuse to act?
When this information was first brought to me I was told the story verbally by a man who came to me and said that he was unable

The Canadian Citizenship Act has a provision that covers the case raised in the house tonight thoroughly and completely. I should like to quote section 41, which is quite clear. It reads:
41. A person who
(a) for any of the purposes of this act knowingly makes any false representation or any statement false in a material particular ... is guilty of an offence and is liable on summary conviction in respect of each offence to imprisonment, with or without hard labour, for a term not exceeding three months.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the precaution was taken in the Canadian Citizenship Act that misrepresentations may be made in applications for citizenship, and if any citizen of Canada or anyone in Canada finds that a false representation has been made in an application for a certificate of citizenship he has the recourse laid down by this parliament, to apply for a warrant of arrest and prove the case before a competent court. Once perjury was established I think the minister would be duty bound to annul the citizenship certificate which he has granted. In this act there is provision for the minister to do precisely that.
I therefore respectfully submit, Mr. Chairman, that the question which the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace has raised may have some merit; I do not know. But if it

We must realize under the citizenship act just what this court is. It is purely a hearing by a commissioner of citizenship. I quote from the Canadian Citizenship Act, section 28, on the question of filing an opposition to an application for naturalization, which is the problem we are now discussing. The section reads:
At any time after the filing of an application for a certificate of citizenship and previous to the hearing of the application, any person objecting to the granting of the certificate to the applicant may file in the court an opposition in which shall be stated the grounds of his objection.
Mr. Chairman, that is the section of the law enacted by this parliament which deals precisely with the problem before us this evening. I believe that its role is essentially educational and that conclusion, I would suggest, is backed up by the fact that the commissioner for the national film board is an outstanding educationist. I think the choice of a man with that background would suggest that the purpose behind the establishment and the continued operation of the national film board is educational.
This, of course, is an unusual function for a federal body, because the federal jurisdiction usually does not concern itself with educational matters. But I think the money


expended in the production and distribution of films for this purpose is making a very worth while and substantial contribution to the over-all educational function.
If the minister is going to make any comments, I think perhaps I would present that as my first question. Am I right in concluding that the function of the national film board is mainly an educational function? Shall I present a series of questions?
As a matter of fact I am really better satisfied with the definitions that are in the National Film Act.

I am asking that for a reason that I shall indicate as I proceed with my observations. More recently the film board has been making a wider international contact, and here again I would agree that it is carrying out an important function. For example, I had a personal contact with the film board office in the city of New York last fall, and I discovered that its films were being used by the Ford television program "Omnibus" which has an audience of some 20 million viewers. If that function is being carried out on a proportionate basis in other countries I think it indicates that the national film board is more than justifying its existence. Again, I should like the minister to give us some idea of the current or expanding activities in this regard. I imagine that there again the function is educational and also promotional, from the standpoint of encouraging tourist interest in Canada, and that would appear to me to be a legitimate function of the film board.
According to the detailed items in the estimates the national film board is moving into the new medium of television at a very rapid rate, and on page 344 we have an item of some $341,000 that will be voted for the production of films for television during the current fiscal year. I am wondering whether this suggests that there is a tendency on the part of the film board to abandon its primary role of an educational operation, and whether in view of the demand for television films there might not be a tendency to commercialize the activities of the board.
As I understand the act and the original purpose of establishing the national film board, it was in no way intended to provide a commercial operation. Yet with the rapidly increasing appropriate for television films it would appear that it might be moving into this commercial activity because of the sheer weight of the demand. I do not have the figures before me, but I understand that commercial film activities in this country have been growing at an astounding rate since C.B.C. television went on the air. It would seem to me that rather than compete with

this very worth-while development in the realm of private activity, it might be advisable to allow the private activity to grow in response to the commercial demand and maintain the essential function of the national film board, namely the educational role.

I think perhaps I might just interrupt the hon. gentleman to read him the purposes that parliament gave the national film board, because I would not like anyone to take my silence as assenting to his proposition that the primary function of the film board is educational in any constitutional sense of the word. This is what the act says:
The board is established to initiate and promote the production and distribution of films In the national interest and in particular
(a) to produce and distribute and to promote the production and distribution of films designed to interpret Canada to Canadians and to other nations . . .
That is the first of the purposes. I do not think I need to read the others. It does seem to me that as between showing films in theatres, showing films in community halls and that sort of place and showing them on television, all these are ways of exhibiting that can accomplish that same purpose.
Quite.
Incidentally, I should add that there is nothing commercial about our television operations. I wish they were more commercial than, in fact, they are.

I think the minister has suggested that the national film board is tending to move into the lucrative field of television and theatrical showings more than was originally intended, and that is the impression I got from the information that was available.
Of course when the film board was set up there was no television, so that could not have been originally intended.

And the film board was set up originally, of course, largely in response to wartime demands for additional information concerning Canada at war. It seems to me that in moving more and more into the commercial phase of films-

I really must deprecate that term. There is nothing commercial about it. The national film board films shown on the C.B.C. are not fully paid for by the C.B.C., so there is nothing that, by the widest stretch of the imagination, can be considered commercial about them. This is just taking advantage of one way of getting these films, the purpose of which is to interpret Canada to Canadians, before Canadians; and I might add that, in spite of the television activity,
Supply-National Film Board the non-theatrical distribution of films last year in Canada was before a total audience of 14,500,000 people. That does not mean 14,500,000 different individuals. The figure is computed in the way they compute the number of people who ride on street cars.

Maybe the word I am using, commercialization, is an unfortunate word, but I repeat my opening remarks that the national film board was established as a government film agency largely to carry out the educational and cultural role to which the minister has referred in reading the definition in the act. I mentioned also at the outset that this is a significant year in the activities of the film board because it is moving to its new $5 million plant.
Has moved.

It has moved to its new $5 million plant in the city of Montreal. I have not had the opportunity to see the facilities, but perhaps that will come at some time in the future when a parliamentary committee is reviewing in detail the operations of the film board. But I imagine that a plant costing that sum of money is capable of producing a fairly substantial quantity of films. I am wondering whether the expansion into this new larger plant facility is an indication that the national film board is going to increasingly extend its activities in the general field of film production.
I raise that point, Mr. Chairman, because there is always a danger in state-operated mass media services. I am sure the commissioner of the national film board, who is an educationalist and who takes the philosophic approach to these things, is quite aware of the danger of an expanding state operation in the field of public information of any kind. In fact, in a speech to a Canadian club audience in London, Ontario last February Dr. Trueman warned the citizens to whom he was speaking that they should be wary of government agencies such as the film board because, as he said:
... it is perfectly possible to use such an agency for propaganda purposes.
Then Dr. Trueman carried on as follows:
I have never seen any indication that this would happen, but it could, and it's a private citizen's democratic responsibility to keep an eye on it.
That is quite a legitimate observation, and I am making it not as a private citizen but as a member of this house. I just wonder whether it is possible to stop the expansion of this public information film service under the direction of the state. It has very wide implications. I am merely expressing this warning or perhaps this hope that there will be no attempt by state-subsidized public

Supply-National Film Board information film services to compete with the healthy and thriving film industry that is emerging in response to the new demands for film for television services.
Before I conclude my observations on this subject, may I say that I have been reading through the 1954-55 report and that it seems to me there is a great deal of what I might call cultural inbreeding in the members of the board. I am wondering whether this is a healthy sign.
Is that a tribute to Mr. Bruce Hutchison?

I am wondering whether this is a further sign that there is not a sufficiently broad control of the activities of the national film board. For example, there are four senior members of various government departments serving on the national film board.
Of course the hon. gentleman realizes that this is required by the statute.

That is fine. I am just making the observation that there are four senior officials out of a total membership of nine, including the commissioner. It is therefore a fairly broad representation from government departments. I am not acquainted with the members of the board other than the editor of the Victoria Daily Times, Mr. Bruce Hutchison. I suppose he is there because of his wide contributions in the field of Canadian letters, particularly in the area of popular history.
He is a Liberal.
Is he a Liberal? I did not know that. The representation from western Canada includes a lady from Saskatoon.
The lady from Saskatoon is no longer there. A lady from Winnipeg has taken the place of the lady from Saskatoon.

That is good. That answers a query that I was going to raise. I was surprised that there was no representation from the city of Winnipeg. We westerners feel that Winnipeg is rapidly becoming the cultural centre of Canada, if it has not already achieved that position. I am not speaking merely from a parochial viewpoint when I say that. We have concrete cultural activities which would tend to back up the point I am making.
The chairman has already had quite an acquaintance with Winnipeg.

Yes. The minister will recall that at the time the great exodus from Ottawa


was contemplated, certain representations were made to the effect that Winnipeg would be the logical and ideal centre because there you have the two cultures, the two languages and so forth, and you also have the western viewpoint which we feel is the real spirit of the new Canada. Unfortunately, because of the geographic location of this important government information activity, there is a tendency to neglect the western regions.
I was glad to hear the minister's reply that an appointment has been made from Winnipeg. I trust that appointment will help to even out the balance in this regard considerably.
In reading the report I was surprised to discover that there was on the board no representatives from the Canadian film society. The Canadian film society was established prior to the national film board. In fact it was what you might call the pioneering group in this particular field of public information in Canada. It was established in 1935 by a group of private citizens. It has continued its operations in the field of film distribution. I myself have had contact with them down through the years.
As far as my own personal experience with them is concerned, I feel that they are the group most qualified to advise and assist in the whole field of film production and distribution in Canada. I think some representation from this important group, which is still functioning as a private society, might help to avoid the danger that is always present when the government is operating in the field of mass media communication, and where it tries to use this media for its own propaganda purposes.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to hold up the committee for more than two minutes, but I should like to bring one thing to the minister's attention with regard to a very eminent Canadian in the province of Ontario. A judge in our country by the name of Eric Cross has written an excellent play called "The Patriots". It deals with the history of this country at the time of Baldwin and Lafontaine. That play has been presented by the London little theatre, Queen's University, and the Woodstock little theatre, and I know it is being considered by others. This play is also required reading in the schools of Ontario. His Honour Judge Cross is an excellent historian and an excellent playwright. He spent a great deal of time in preparing this play. I might say that Judge Cross was formerly the attorney general of the province of Ontario, was minister of education of Ontario for a while, and also minister of municipal affairs.
Mr. Chairman, I may not be much of a judge of painting, but I consider that I have

some slight knowledge and appreciation of the theatre. I might say that this play by any standards, either from the historical point of view or from the straight theatre point of view, would be difficult to improve upon. I would rather hope that perhaps the minister might consider sending instructions to the national film board that they might consider this play as a subject to be filmed for use in Canadian schools or something of that nature. The very fact the province of Ontario has made this play required reading is, I think, a recommendation in itself.
I shall be delighted to draw that fact to the attention of the film board and ask them to give it most careful consideration.
Like Sergeant Friday in "Dragnet" I should like a little bit of information. Can the minister tell the committee what would be the total cost of the new building and equipment in Montreal?

I have it right here. The amount provided from the funds of the national film board for the purchase of new equipment and the relocation of existing equipment was $1,446,503, over the period from the time this move started to the present. The amount for the Ottawa headquarters was $21,632; for technical services to overcome shut-downs, $114,554; for the removal of staff-that does not come directly within the question, but perhaps the hon. member might want all the information- $202,905; for recruiting, training, travelling and other expenses, $123,186, making a total cost of the move to the film board of $1,908,780.

The
minister is doing marvellously with his second sight because that was my second question, the total cost of the move to Montreal. He has answered that, although I have not put the question. My first question was the total cost of the new building and equipment.

I am afraid, sir, it would perhaps be inappropriate for me to transgress on the field of another minister. My department did not build the building, but I am told that the total cost-it is not quite complete in every detail-and since this is a public works figure I do not guarantee it, but that the total cost including furniture, fixtures, purchase of the site and public works share of the move was $6,400,000; that is approximate, but it is very close.
Supply-National Film Board

That is very kind of the minister and I appreciate it. Has he any idea of the increase in the cost of administration because of this new building? I have in mind such things as maintenance; the necessity for separate Ottawa offices; the necessity to travel between the two cities and the necessity, for example, to have a number of new positions such as, I understand, a new deputy commissioner, which post has been or will be created. Can he estimate those additional costs?

The apparent cost, as the hon. gentleman will realize, is considerably greater than the real additional cost, for this reason. In Ottawa certain services are provided by public works and by the Department of Finance, such as telephones, caretakers, cleaners and so on, which have to be provided by the film board in Montreal. The figure I am given of the estimated total increased cost for 1956-57 as a result of the move and the fact that there are two offices would be $97,929, that is to say very nearly $100,000.	1 want to emphasize again that
some of this is only an apparent increase.

The
figure of $97,000 is a very real one, though, to some of us taxpayers. Can the minister tell the house if the government has taken into consideration the recent United Kingdom experience, where they have closed down, I understand, the British equivalent to the national film board, their production division known as Crown Films? I am wondering if he knows of that and if it might have some reflection on the operations of this national film board. Has he studied that British policy?

I understand that the
Crown Films unit, to which I presume the hon. gentleman refers, was closed several years before I became minister in charge of this board. I have no doubt my predecessor did take account of any experience the United Kingdom government may have had as a result.

Can
the minister tell us whether the commissioner of the film board is now going to reside in Ottawa? If so, how much time will he spend in Montreal where the operation is centralized?

I think it would be premature-the commissioner is going to reside in Ottawa, and unfortunately he is going to spend a large amount of time travelling, from what he has already told me, though I hope once things get running more smoothly he

Supply-National Film Board can reduce this a little and spend more time keeping the minister informed about what is happening. There are going to be certain difficulties about this which were thoroughly appreciated by the government at the time the decision was made. I do not think it will be possible to say even approximately the amount of time the commissioner will have to spend in Montreal until there has been several months or perhaps a year's experience in that operation.
Does the minister still feel the move to Montreal is justified, in view of the fact that all the film board customers are in Ottawa and the commissioner himself is residing in Ottawa?

I should like to reserve my answer to that question until a year from now or, I hope, something less than a year from now, when we have had a little more experience on which I could base it. My feeling would be that it is, but I think it would be rather presumptuous of me to express an opinion before we have had a little more experience.

Can
the minister tell us what per cent of the board's production last year was for C.B.C. account, either in dollars or in number of feet?
It is somewhere between 30 per cent and 40 per cent of the total production costs.

So
in the past year between 30 per cent and 40 per cent of the national film board production costs were for C.B.C.?
But that does not mean that proportion of the budget went for that, because some of that cost was recovered from the C.B.C.

Do
I understand that you do not recover the full costs from C.B.C.?
No.

I do
not want to get into a long discussion on this national film board, but to a certain extent it is subsidizing certain aspects of C.B.C. operations?
That would be one way to describe it, and I will not quarrel with the term.

Can
the minister tell us, looking ahead to next year, what per cent of their production they would expect would be for the C.B.C. on the same basis as last year?

Roughly about the same, but that will be subject to audit later. That is the present expectation. Incidentally I might add, and I think the hon. gentleman will be interested, that the amount provided for the film board for production has not been increased this year over last year or last year over the previous year.

My
final question on this score, Mr. Chairman, is whether the minister would like to comment on what the government's thinking might be about the future relationship between the national film board and the C.B.C.?

I think it would be most undesirable for me to do so at this time. I am very hopeful that one of the things that will be considered by the Fowler commission is the relationship between these two agencies. I would not wish to express views here which might in any way seem to prejudge that question. I think there are some problems in this area that need to be solved.

can understand why the minister finds it difficult to comment at this point but in view of his hesitation to comment would he say whether or not he approves of the present policy under which the national film board is doing work for the C.B.C. at less than cost in some cases?

Well, sir, that is a really embarrassing question. I have the responsibility to parliament for the film board and I would love to have the full cost paid by the C.B.C., but I do not know whether I can persuade my colleague the Minister of National Revenue to persuade the C.B.C. to do it. This is precisely one of those problems on which some further thinking needs to be done.
Mr. Chairman, may I just point out to the minister how much more easily we got along this time when he had his officials sitting in front of him.
The minister realizes his own limitations.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to take just about one minute to tell the minister and the committee of an experience that several hon. members, along with the distinguished Clerk of this house had in touring South Africa two years ago next month. One sunny morning about 25 miles outside of Capetown when driving along the seacoast on the beautiful Cape peninsula we stopped at an inn. Outside was a board advertising the showing of certain films the following day in a community hall

nearby. On the delighted eyes of these Canadians, 14,000 miles from home, fell these Canadian titles:	"The Loon's Necklace,"
"Barbara Ann Scott", "The Mounties get their Man". These were three films distributed by the national film board.
On inquiry we were told that the films of the national film board have a very large circulation in South Africa. That circulation has been promoted actively, I know, by the Canadian trade commissioner at Capetown.
I thank the hon. gentleman very much. Those films are all excellent, as he and I both know.

Mr. Chairman, in all fairness to the private film industry of Canada may I point out that "The Loon's Necklace" at least is not a production of the national film board but of one of the great private producers in Canada which has a distinguished reputation, Crawley Films Limited.
I am delighted the hon. member has pointed that out, because one of the principal objects of the national film board is to promote and encourage the private film industry in Canada.

This item has to do with the St. Lawrence seaway project. The other night when the estimates were up the minister promised that he would deal with a question asked by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace under the St. Lawrence seaway item.

I certainly do not want to avoid fulfilling my commitment to the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, but I suggest that this is not the appropriate item.
