Has the minister given any consideration to bringing the administration of all canals under the seaway authority?

It will probably not be until the navigation year 1959 that the seaway will be open for shipping and the question of the administration of the canal system generally would not arise. I can tell my hon. friend that there is a provision in the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act whereby the governor in council may transfer the administration of canals which are contributory to the seaway system to the authority. As the hon. gentleman probably knows, there are canals which would not fall into that category and which are under the administration of the Department of Transport. In my opinion it is desirable that the whole attention of the St. Lawrence seaway authority should be devoted to the seaway itself and not to what might be considered problems of administration.

I am referring to the canals which will provide a link between the great lakes and the ocean. There will be ships of foreign registry plying the inland waters, and since we are endeavouring to remove all obstacles to ships travelling from the ocean to the head of the lakes I think we should try to streamline the administration and have foreign and Canadian vessels come under the one authority. While this may not be the time to discuss the matter I am wondering if any thought has been given to it. I think this would be the proper solution for traffic over our inland waters.

Item agreed to.
Marine services-
440. Marine services administration, including agencies, $670,240.
I understand that this is the item under which the search and rescue service is provided. Could the minister tell us the present situation with regard to that service?

For some reason or other which has always puzzled me when anybody mentions the subject of search and rescue he always seems to direct his attention to me. While I may be flattered by the attention I get in this way, the fact does remain that this is the primary responsibility of the Department of National Defence and the co-ordination is carried out by the Department of National Defence.
As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra knows, the facilities of all departments which operate sea-going vessels are

part and parcel of the search and rescue organization. We have a number of ships, and I suppose for that reason when the subject of search and rescue is mentioned everybody looks to the Department of Transport and seems to imply that the problem of search and rescue is exclusively one of transport. I do not think that is the situation as search and rescue is organized at the present time. All we do is play our part in providing ships where agency vessels may be used in the process, and also to facilitate the problem of communications.
I think the hon. member is fully aware of the situation as to search and rescue generally, and I do not think I can say anything more on this particular item than that our departmental vessels are available when they can be of service.

Which department has the primary responsibility for the operation and extension of this service? Surely there must be one department of government which has that responsibility. Somebody has to be in charge; the Minister of National Defence or some minister must be responsible for the planning and extension of this service. As the minister knows, it has been in operation for only a short time and improvements will have to be made as the years go by. I suggest that some minister should be given this responsibility. It is quite true that there are several departments co-operating, but somebody should be the leader.
I have suggested that a proper coastguard service should be established, but the government has rejected that plan for this search and rescue plan. What I am concerned about is who is the responsible minister for seeing that this becomes a thoroughly efficient service. I do not think it is wise to have it under four or five different ministers.

I thought in my remarks a moment ago I had said plainly that the primary responsibility rested on the Department of National Defence. As the hon. gentleman knows, I think, that department co-ordinates the search and rescue activities of the navy, when the navy can be of assistance, and the air force and all the various other departments, and of the ships which may be somewhere in the vicinity of the need and which may respond to it, but the responsibility for co-ordination and correction, as I understand it, rests with the Department of National Defence.
Are there any plans in mind for the extension of this service?

I think that would have been a good question for the hon. member to put to the Minister of National Defence when
Supply-Transport
his estimates were under consideration. I can only speak insofar as my own department is concerned. I shall say to the hon. member that we have been considering whether in the design of our agency vessels we can make some changes which would make them better suited for carrying out search and rescue operations where it is possible to do so.
The hon. member mentioned the subject of coastguards. He is probably fully familiar with the situation in the United States, but those who are continually preaching the idea of a Canadian coastguard on the lines of the United States coastguard must remember that the United States spends something of the order of $125 million a year just for this coastguard service. They carry out a number of functions that are carried out in Canada by various departments. For example, as I understand the origin of the United States coastguard, it was designed primarily for revenue purposes, to control smuggling. That is not a function now of the Department of Transport; it is carried out by the R.C.M.P. The question of the supply of buoys, the sort of work that is carried out through marine service for the Department of Transport, is likewise done by the United States coastguard. They go in for icebreaking, as we do. They have some of the functions of the Department of Transport, some of the R.C.M.P. and some of other departments. What is perhaps unfortunate is that it is difficult for any single individual to specify all the single services of any one department which it might be described as those of a coastguard.
Is there any civil servant who has the responsibility for heading up the search and rescue service, or is it merely a matter of co-operation among the departments?
That is a question the hon. member should have put on the estimates of the Department of National Defence.

There is no vote under the Department of National Defence for a search and rescue service as such. Does the minister not think it would be advantageous to organize this service in such a way that it would come under the direction of some particular minister and some particular deputy?

I hope the hon. gentleman does not ask me to repeat what I have already said twice; that is, that the primary responsibility rests under the Department of National Defence. I have 95 or 96 items in my budget and I am quite prepared to deal with those,

Supply-Transport
but I do not wish to add the items of the Department of National Defence to the 95 I already have.

May I say this in supplementing what the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has just said. The minister tells us that questions with respect to the coastguard or search and rescue should have been asked in connection with the Department of National Defence.
I am saying rescue, not coastguard.

As the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra has said, there is no item in the defence estimates where we could have possibly asked that question. This is a matter I have raised for many years, and I must say that the present minister is much more modest than his predecessor, because his predecessor at one time took the responsibility for the fact that he was co-ordinating all the ships of his department and those of national defence and fisheries into what he said was equal to, if not better than, the coastguard service of the United States.
Those of us from the eastern seaboard, at any rate, have been much concerned about this for many years. There have been cases where the minister, if he looks back or has some of his staff go back through the debates in Hansard on this matter in years gone by, will find that this was raised. I have spent considerable time and given instance after instance where a coastguard service would have been of incalculable value.
Now we have a situation where the minister says, perhaps rightly, he has a great many items, but he has no item here for a coastguard. After all he is the Minister of Transport. His predecessors at any rate took some responsibility in this matter. We know that search and rescue operations were carried out by the air force operating out of Greenwood, Nova Scotia, and nowhere was there a more efficient search and rescue operation carried on than by the air force. But the air force cannot cover the whole field expected of a coastguard service. You cannot land planes in rough water, and so on. We saw an example in the recent disaster when the Andrea Doria collided with the Swedish ship. The United States coastguard was co-ordinating the rescue services, although the French liner and others took a primary part in it.
On the east coast we have had casualty after casualty over a period of many years. We thought at least there would be some co-ordination in dealing with the various services. The minister says it comes under

the Department of National Defence, and apparently we should have asked the question of the Minister of National Defence about that. I say that the place to ask the question is on the estimates of the Minister of Transport, who at least in so far as his department is concerned three years ago took full responsibility for the way in which this should be handled and co-ordinated. He laughed to scorn those of us who said that there should be a coastguard service, and he said we had operating in co-ordination with the Department of National Defence a much more efficient service, or so he implied, than was operated by the coastguard service in the United States. I am not satisfied with this brush-off, and I say that with respect.
